en.q: Per the IRC, how much should the finished grade fall away from a foundation within the first 10 feet?
o: At least 2 inches
At least 3 inches
At least 6 inches
At least 12 inches
en.e: Per the IRC (R401.3), the grade should fall at least 6 inches within the first 10 feet (about a 5% slope) so that surface water drains away from the foundation.

en.q: An inspector sees soil sloping toward the house along one wall, and the basement wall on that side shows white mineral deposits and a damp stain. What is the most appropriate report entry?
o: State that the foundation is failing and recommend immediate replacement by a contractor
Report the negative grading and moisture signs; recommend regrading away from the house
Make no comment, because grading is a landscaping matter outside the scope of the inspection
Recommend that the client install a dehumidifier in the basement and take no other action
en.e: Grading that slopes toward the house is a common cause of basement moisture. The inspector should report it with the related evidence and recommend correcting the drainage. Nothing observed supports calling the foundation failed.

en.q: Per the IRC, impervious surfaces such as concrete walks within 10 feet of the building should slope away from it at a minimum of:
o: 2 percent
0.5 percent
5 percent
10 percent
en.e: Per the IRC (R401.3), impervious surfaces within 10 feet of the foundation may slope at not less than 2 percent away from the building. The 6-inch-in-10-feet (5%) rule applies to soil.

en.q: A downspout empties directly against the foundation at a corner where the basement shows water staining. What should the inspector recommend?
o: Sealing the inside of the basement wall with waterproof paint to stop the leaks
Removing the gutter system, because gutters concentrate water and cause foundation leaks
Extending the downspout so that it discharges well away from the foundation
Filling the area around the downspout with gravel and leaving the discharge where it is
en.e: Roof water concentrated at the foundation is a frequent cause of basement leaks and settlement. Downspouts should discharge several feet from the foundation or into an approved drainage system. Interior sealers do not fix the source.

en.q: Per the IRC, what is the minimum clearance between wood siding and the ground, unless the wood is naturally durable or preservative-treated?
o: 2 inches
4 inches
6 inches
8 inches
en.e: Per the IRC (R317.1), wood siding, sheathing and wall framing on the exterior must be at least 6 inches above the ground (and at least 2 inches above concrete steps, patios and similar surfaces) unless decay-resistant wood is used.

en.q: Per the IRC, the weep screed at the bottom of an exterior stucco wall should be at least how far above earth and above paved areas?
o: 1 inch above earth and 1 inch above paving
4 inches above earth and 2 inches above paving
6 inches above earth and 4 inches above paving
8 inches above earth and 6 inches above paving
en.e: Per the IRC (R703.7.2.1), the foundation weep screed must be at least 4 inches above the earth or 2 inches above paved areas so that water behind the stucco can drain.

en.q: Per the IRC, weep holes in the outer wythe of brick veneer must be spaced no more than how far apart?
o: 16 inches on center
24 inches on center
33 inches on center
48 inches on center
en.e: Per the IRC (R703.8.6), weep holes are required immediately above the flashing at a maximum spacing of 33 inches on center, with a minimum diameter of 3/16 inch.

en.q: At the base of a brick veneer wall, the inspector cannot find any weep holes, and the bottom course is buried in mulch. What is the main concern?
o: Water behind the veneer cannot drain and may damage sheathing and framing
The brick will expand and crack because the wall cannot breathe without weeps
Rodents and insects will enter the wall cavity through the buried openings
The mortar joints will cure too slowly and remain soft for many years
en.e: Brick veneer is a drainage wall: water that penetrates it must run down the air space and out through weeps above the flashing. Without weeps, or with them buried, the water is trapped against the wood structure.

en.q: What are the minimum diameter and the location of weep holes in brick veneer per the IRC?
o: 1/8 inch, at mid-height of the wall
3/16 inch, immediately above the flashing
1/2 inch, just below the sill plate
3/4 inch, at the top course under the eave
en.e: Per the IRC (R703.8.6), weep holes must be at least 3/16 inch in diameter and located immediately above the flashing, where water collected by the flashing exits.

en.q: An inspector finds barrier-type EIFS (synthetic stucco) that extends into the soil, with no kickout flashing where a roof edge meets the wall. Soft spots are felt below the roof-wall intersection. What is the most appropriate action?
o: Report the cladding as acceptable, because EIFS is a waterproof barrier system
Cut open the wall in the soft area to confirm rot before writing the report
Report the conditions and refer to a qualified EIFS specialist for moisture testing
Recommend recoating the EIFS with elastomeric paint to seal out the moisture
en.e: Barrier EIFS cannot drain water that gets behind it, so hidden damage is common at roof-wall intersections and where the cladding meets grade. Destructive testing is beyond a home inspection; the correct step is referral to a specialist.

en.q: Vinyl siding shows waviness and buckled panels on a sunny wall. What installation error most likely caused this?
o: Spacing the nails too far apart along the nailing hem
Leaving small gaps at the ends of panels where they meet trim
Driving the nails tight against the panels
Installing the siding over house wrap instead of directly over sheathing
en.e: Vinyl siding moves a lot with temperature. It must hang loosely on its nails with room to expand at the ends; nails driven tight pin the panels and cause buckling.

en.q: A deck ledger is fastened to the house only with nails and has no flashing above it. What should the inspector report?
o: That the ledger is acceptable as long as the nails are hot-dip galvanized and closely spaced
That the deck will perform well once a bead of caulk is added along the top of the ledger
That the attachment and flashing are deficient and need correction by a qualified contractor
That the ledger only needs to be painted or stained so that water cannot soak into it
en.e: Ledger failure is a leading cause of deck collapse. Ledgers should be attached with lag screws or through-bolts (or another approved method) and flashed to keep water out of the house band joist. Nails alone are not an acceptable attachment.

en.q: Per the IRC, a deck ledger may NOT be supported on which of these?
o: A preservative-treated band joist
A solid concrete foundation wall
Brick or stone veneer
A properly sized dimensional-lumber rim joist
en.e: Per the IRC (R507.9.2), deck ledgers must not be supported on stone or masonry veneer, because veneer is not designed to carry structural loads. A freestanding deck is the usual alternative.

en.q: Per the IRC, guards are required on a deck when the walking surface is more than how far above the grade below, measured within 36 inches horizontally of the edge?
o: 18 inches
24 inches
30 inches
42 inches
en.e: Per the IRC (R312.1.1), guards are required where the walking surface is more than 30 inches above the floor or grade below at any point within 36 inches horizontally of the edge.

en.q: Deck balusters are spaced so that a 5-inch ball passes between them. The deck is 6 feet above the yard. How should this be reported?
o: As acceptable, because the IRC limit for openings is 6 inches
As a safety hazard, because guard openings should not pass a 4-inch sphere per the IRC
As acceptable, because baluster spacing rules apply only to interior stairs
As a cosmetic issue that needs no recommendation
en.e: Per the IRC (R312.1.3), openings in guards must not allow a 4-inch sphere to pass. Wider spacing lets small children slip through, so it is a safety item.

en.q: Several deck joist hangers have empty nail holes, and some are fastened with drywall screws. What is the best report comment?
o: The hangers are adequate as long as each one has at least one fastener on each side
Drywall screws are harder than nails, so using them is an upgrade over the original nailing
The hangers are not fastened as the manufacturer requires and need correction
The joists should be glued into the hangers with construction adhesive to stiffen them
en.e: Joist hangers reach their rated capacity only with the specified fasteners in the specified holes. Drywall screws are brittle and are not rated for structural shear loads.

en.q: Per the IRC, fasteners and connectors used with preservative-treated lumber should be:
o: Plain steel, because the preservative in the wood also protects the metal
Aluminum, because it is lighter and does not rust like steel
Hot-dip galvanized or stainless steel
Electro-galvanized drywall screws, because their coating resists rust
en.e: Per the IRC (R317.3), fasteners in preservative-treated wood must be hot-dip zinc-coated galvanized steel, stainless steel, silicon bronze or copper (with limited exceptions). Modern treatments corrode plain and lightly coated steel.

en.q: A 5-foot-tall landscape retaining wall near the house leans outward, bulges in the middle and has no visible drainage outlets. What is the most likely cause?
o: The wall was built too thick for the amount of soil it holds
Water and soil pressure behind a poorly drained wall
Too much direct sunlight on the face of the wall during the summer
The mortar was mixed with too much lime, making it too strong
en.e: Water trapped behind a retaining wall adds a lot of pressure. Leaning and bulging point to inadequate drainage or design. The inspector should report it and recommend evaluation by a qualified professional, such as an engineer.

en.q: Per the IRC, retaining walls that are not laterally supported at the top must be designed for stability when they retain more than how much unbalanced fill?
o: 24 inches
36 inches
48 inches
72 inches
en.e: Per the IRC (R404.4), retaining walls not laterally supported at the top that retain more than 48 inches of unbalanced fill must be designed against overturning, sliding and excessive soil pressure.

en.q: Large tree limbs hang over the roof and rub the shingles. What is the most appropriate report comment?
o: Leave it out, because trees are outside the scope of every standard of practice
Recommend removing all trees within 50 feet of the house to protect the foundation
Note the risk of roof damage and recommend trimming by a qualified tree service
State that the tree is diseased and is likely to fall on the house in the next storm
en.e: Standards of practice include vegetation that is likely to adversely affect the building. The inspector reports the effect and recommends trimming, without diagnosing tree health, which is outside the inspector's expertise.

en.q: Under typical home inspection standards of practice, which of these is the inspector NOT required to inspect?
o: Driveways and walkways next to the house
Exterior wall coverings
Grading and drainage that may affect the building
Swimming pools, spas and fences
en.e: Typical standards of practice (such as ASHI and InterNACHI) cover wall coverings, flashing, trim, walkways, drives and the grading and vegetation that affect the building. Pools, spas, fences and other recreational facilities are excluded unless separately agreed.

en.q: Per the IRC, what is the minimum horizontal area of a window well that serves an emergency escape window?
o: 5.7 square feet
9 square feet
12 square feet
16 square feet
en.e: Per the IRC (R310.2.3.1 in the 2021 edition), a window well serving an emergency escape opening needs at least 9 square feet of horizontal area, with a minimum horizontal projection and width of 36 inches.

en.q: Per the IRC, an egress window well needs a permanently attached ladder or steps when its vertical depth is more than:
o: 24 inches
36 inches
44 inches
60 inches
en.e: Per the IRC, a window well deeper than 44 inches needs a permanently affixed ladder or steps that remain usable with the window fully open. The ladder must not intrude more than 6 inches into the required dimensions of the well.

en.q: A basement window well is full of leaves and standing water, and the window frame below it is stained. What is the most appropriate recommendation?
o: Seal the window shut with caulk so that water in the well cannot leak inside
Clean the well, restore its drainage, consider a cover, and check the window
Fill the well with soil up to the bottom of the window to keep water out of it
No action, because window wells are designed to hold water after a heavy rain
en.e: A clogged window well collects water against the window. Restoring drainage, keeping debris out and checking the window address the cause. Sealing an egress window shut would create a safety problem.

en.q: Per the IRC, a door between an attached garage and the house may be which of these?
o: A hollow-core wood door of any thickness
A solid wood door at least 1-3/8 inches thick
A sliding glass door
Any door, as long as it has weatherstripping
en.e: Per the IRC (R302.5.1), openings between the garage and the residence need solid wood or solid or honeycomb-core steel doors at least 1-3/8 inches thick, or 20-minute fire-rated doors. Since the 2018 edition the IRC also requires a self-closing or automatic-closing device.

en.q: The door from the garage into the house is a hollow-core interior door. How should the inspector report this?
o: As acceptable, because any closed door slows the spread of a garage fire
As a cosmetic issue to be handled whenever the door is next replaced
As a fire-separation deficiency needing a compliant door
As acceptable as long as a working smoke alarm is installed in the garage
en.e: The garage-to-house door is part of the fire separation. A hollow-core door does not provide the required resistance, so the inspector should report it as a safety item.

en.q: Per the IRC, which opening is NOT permitted between an attached garage and the dwelling?
o: A door from the garage directly into a bedroom
A door from the garage into a mudroom
A door from the garage into a kitchen
A door from the garage into a hallway
en.e: Per the IRC (R302.5.1), openings from a private garage directly into a room used for sleeping are not permitted.

en.q: Per the IRC, when there is a habitable room above an attached garage, the garage ceiling must have at least:
o: 1/2-inch regular gypsum board
3/8-inch gypsum board
5/8-inch Type X gypsum board
1/2-inch plywood
en.e: Per the IRC (Table R302.6), the garage side of walls needs at least 1/2-inch gypsum board, but where there is habitable space above the garage the ceiling needs at least 5/8-inch Type X gypsum board.

en.q: When the automatic garage door is tested, it does not reverse after it contacts an object on the floor. What is the most appropriate report entry?
o: Report it as a safety hazard and recommend repair by a qualified technician
Report it as normal wear for openers and doors that are more than 10 years old
Recommend that the occupants keep children and pets out of the garage instead
Disconnect the opener so that it cannot be used and leave it out of the report
en.e: Automatic openers are designed to reverse when the door meets an obstruction. A failure to reverse can cause serious injury, so it is a safety finding that needs correction.

en.q: The photo-eye sensors for an automatic garage door are mounted about 4 feet above the floor. Why is this a concern?
o: The sensors wear out faster when they are mounted far above the floor
The door will refuse to close at all until the sensors are lowered
A child or pet below the beam may not be detected
The sensors may be confused by light from the garage ceiling fixtures
en.e: Photo-eye safety sensors are meant to sense small objects near the floor; manufacturers and the UL 325 standard call for them to be mounted no more than about 6 inches above the floor.

en.q: In winter, a hose is still attached to a frost-free hose bibb. What risk should the inspector mention?
o: The hose bibb will leak into the yard because the hose keeps its washer compressed
The hose will make the bibb drip continuously and waste water all winter long
Water held in the bibb can freeze and split the pipe inside the wall
The attached hose will reduce water pressure to the other fixtures throughout the house
en.e: A frost-free bibb works by draining the section of pipe in the cold wall. An attached hose keeps water in the valve, which can freeze and burst it inside the wall, where the leak may go unnoticed.

en.q: The inspector notices peeling paint and a soft-looking exterior window sill. What is an appropriate way to check it?
o: Remove the sill and the trim below it to look at the wall framing behind them
Gently probe the suspect area with an awl, without damaging sound finishes
Leave it out of the report, because rot can only be confirmed by laboratory tests
Tap the sill firmly with a hammer to see whether the wood breaks apart or holds
en.e: Standards such as ASHI's call for probing where deterioration is suspected, but not where probing would damage finished surfaces that appear sound. A soft sill can be checked carefully and reported.

en.q: A concrete sidewalk slab has heaved and now has a 1-inch lip where it meets the next slab. How should this be reported?
o: As cosmetic only
As a trip hazard, recommending correction
As a sign of foundation failure
As a code violation that requires a permit
en.e: A raised edge in a walking path is a trip hazard and should be reported as a safety item. A heaved walk alone does not show a problem with the house foundation.

en.q: Per the IRC, the landing at an exterior door must measure at least how far in the direction of travel?
o: 24 inches
36 inches
42 inches
48 inches
en.e: Per the IRC (R311.3), the floor or landing on each side of an exterior door must be at least as wide as the door and at least 36 inches in the direction of travel.

en.q: An exterior door does not swing over its outside landing. Per the IRC, how far below the top of the threshold may that landing be?
o: No more than 1-1/2 inches
No more than 4 inches
No more than 7-3/4 inches
No more than 12 inches
en.e: Per the IRC (R311.3.1), the exterior landing may be no more than 7-3/4 inches below the top of the threshold, provided the door does not swing over it. That is the same as the maximum riser height.

en.q: Fiber-cement siding was installed down to the soil and tight against a roof surface. What is the best basis for reporting this?
o: No comment is needed, because fiber cement does not absorb water or decay
It does not meet the manufacturer's clearance instructions
Fiber cement must always be at least 18 inches above grade under every code
Fiber cement may never be installed on any wall that is next to a roof surface
en.e: Fiber-cement products can be damaged by constant moisture, and manufacturers specify clearances to grade, hard surfaces and roofs. Reporting a departure from the manufacturer's instructions is defensible and specific.

en.q: Mulch has been piled against the house so that it covers the bottom of the wood siding. What two problems does this create?
o: Higher water pressure at the hose bibbs and lower heating bills in winter
Wood decay and a hidden termite path
Faster paint drying, along with color fading of the lower siding courses
Better drainage of roof water and extra insulation for the foundation wall
en.e: Soil or mulch against wood cladding keeps it wet and hides termite entry points. Clearance between cladding and grade should be restored.

en.q: What is the main purpose of head flashing (drip cap) above a window in a siding wall?
o: To support the weight of the siding courses that run above the window opening
To shed water running down the wall away from the window head
To keep insects and nesting birds from getting into the top of the window frame
To cover the gap between the window and the siding for a neater appearance
en.e: Head flashing intercepts water running down the wall and sheds it over the window trim. If it is missing, water can get behind the trim and into the framing.

en.q: Cement shingle siding on a 1950s house may contain asbestos. What is the most appropriate way to report it?
o: State in the report that the siding contains asbestos and must be removed
Break off a small piece of siding and send it to a laboratory for analysis
Describe the siding and note that only lab testing can confirm asbestos
Leave it out of the report, because environmental hazards may not be mentioned
en.e: Standards of practice do not require the inspector to identify environmental hazards. Taking samples could release fibers. Describing the material and advising that testing is needed for confirmation is accurate and within scope.

en.q: Stucco below several windows shows cracks with brown staining underneath. What is the most appropriate recommendation?
o: Painting over the stains with a stain-blocking primer and matching paint
Filling the cracks with caulk and taking no further action on the stains
Evaluation by a qualified stucco or moisture specialist
Removing all of the stucco from the house and replacing it with vinyl siding
en.e: Stains below window corners often indicate leaks at the window flashing that can cause hidden damage. Specialists can do invasive moisture testing, which is beyond a visual inspection.

en.q: A wooden privacy fence is attached directly to the house siding. What is the main concern?
o: The fence will make the house look smaller and lower its curb appeal
The fence will raise the property taxes because it counts as an addition
It can give termites a hidden path and keep the siding wet
The fence will block the electric meter and the utility will refuse to read it
en.e: Wood that bridges from the ground to the house can carry moisture and give wood-destroying insects a path into the structure. Separating the fence from the house is a common recommendation.

en.q: A lawn sprinkler head sprays the lower part of a wood-sided wall every morning. What is the best recommendation?
o: Install a gutter at the bottom of the wall
Adjust the sprinkler so that it does not wet the house
Paint the siding every year
Remove all landscaping
en.e: Repeated wetting of siding and the foundation encourages rot, staining and moisture entry. Redirecting the spray removes the source.

en.q: An inspector is asked to describe the exterior. Which of these is an exterior item that standards of practice typically require the inspector to inspect?
o: The condition of a detached shed
Window screens and storm windows
Eaves, soffits and fascia
Outdoor cooking appliances
en.e: Eaves, soffits and fascia are part of the exterior that standards of practice cover. Outbuildings, screens, storm windows and outdoor cooking equipment are commonly excluded.

en.q: Shrubs are growing against the siding on the north side of the house, and the siding there is green with algae. What is the best recommendation?
o: Trim the vegetation back so that the wall can dry and be inspected
Remove the siding on that wall and replace it with brick veneer instead
Plant more shrubs along the wall to shade it from the afternoon sun
No action, because algae growth shows that the siding is healthy and sound
en.e: Vegetation against the house keeps the wall damp and hides defects and pest activity. Keeping plants trimmed back is standard advice.

en.q: A cracked concrete driveway has hairline cracks but no displacement or trip edges. What is the most accurate description?
o: A structural defect that should be evaluated by a structural engineer
Typical shrinkage cracking, usually of little concern
Evidence that a sinkhole is forming under the driveway and the garage
A sign that the house foundation is failing and moving toward the street
en.e: Concrete flatwork almost always develops shrinkage cracks. Without displacement, trip edges or drainage problems, hairline cracks are usually minor.

en.q: Which observation best indicates a surface drainage problem next to the foundation?
o: Soil erosion channels and water marks running toward the house
A well-sloped lawn
Downspout extensions that reach 6 feet from the house
A dry crawl space with a vapor retarder
en.e: Erosion channels, water marks and puddling at the foundation show that water flows toward the house rather than away from it.

en.q: A brick wall shows white, powdery deposits near the bottom. What do these deposits usually indicate?
o: Mold growing on the face of the bricks because of shade
Termites tunneling through the mortar joints of the wall
Salts left behind by water moving through the masonry
Fire damage from a past fire that scorched the wall surface
en.e: White, powdery deposits on masonry are efflorescence: salts that water carried through the masonry and left on the surface as it evaporated. The deposits show moisture movement. The source should be found.

en.q: Deck stairs have no handrail and five risers. What does the IRC require?
o: No handrail, because stairs serving decks are exempt from handrail rules
A handrail on at least one side
A handrail on both sides of every exterior stair regardless of the number of risers
A handrail only if the stairs are more than 6 feet wide or more than 10 risers tall
en.e: Per the IRC (R311.7.8), handrails are required on at least one side of each flight of stairs with four or more risers. Exterior deck stairs are included.

en.q: A deck's wood posts sit directly on the soil, and their bases are soft and decayed. What is the best recommendation?
o: Paint or stain the posts to seal the decayed wood against further moisture
Repair by a qualified contractor, with posts set on proper footings
Add more posts beside the decayed ones, set directly on the soil without footings
No action, because wood posts are expected to rot slowly and are still adequate
en.e: Posts in direct contact with soil decay, and decayed posts can fail. Posts should bear on footings and be protected from ground moisture; a contractor should repair them.

en.q: A home inspector is asked by the buyer whether the lot is in a flood zone. What is the most appropriate response?
o: Give an opinion based on the slope of the street and the yard around the house
Guarantee in writing that the house will not flood during the client's ownership
Explain it is outside the inspection and suggest flood maps or the insurer
Say that every lot within a mile of a creek or river is in a flood zone
en.e: Determining flood zone status, geological conditions and soil stability is outside a standard home inspection. Referring the client to the proper source avoids giving an unsupported opinion.

en.q: Per the IRC, what is the minimum roof slope for asphalt shingles?
o: 1 unit vertical in 12 horizontal (1:12)
2 units vertical in 12 horizontal (2:12)
3 units vertical in 12 horizontal (3:12)
4 units vertical in 12 horizontal (4:12)
en.e: Per the IRC (R905.2.2), asphalt shingles may be used only on roof slopes of 2:12 or greater. Slopes from 2:12 up to less than 4:12 need double underlayment.

en.q: Per the IRC, asphalt shingles on a slope of 3:12 require:
o: No underlayment
A single layer of underlayment, the same as steeper roofs
Two layers of underlayment (double underlayment)
A fully adhered membrane over the whole roof, with no shingles
en.e: Per the IRC, shingles on slopes from 2:12 to less than 4:12 need two layers of underlayment, because water drains more slowly and wind can drive it under low-slope shingles.

en.q: Per the IRC, where an ice barrier is required, it must extend from the lowest edges of the roof to a point at least how far inside the exterior wall line?
o: 6 inches
12 inches
24 inches
36 inches
en.e: Per the IRC (R905.1.2), in areas with a history of ice damming the ice barrier must run from the eave to at least 24 inches inside the exterior wall line of the building.

en.q: Per the IRC, a new layer of asphalt shingles may NOT be installed over the existing roof (re-covered) when:
o: The existing roof has one layer of shingles
The existing roof already has two or more layers
The existing shingles are less than 10 years old
The roof slope is greater than 6:12
en.e: Per the IRC (R908.3.1.1), re-covering is not permitted where the existing roof has two or more applications of any type of roof covering, so a roof normally has at most two layers.

en.q: Per the IRC, which existing roof covering may NOT be covered over with new shingles, even if it is the only layer?
o: A single layer of asphalt shingles in good condition
Wood shakes, slate or clay tile
A single layer of fiberglass three-tab shingles
Architectural asphalt shingles that lie flat
en.e: Per the IRC (R908.3.1.1), re-covering is not permitted over wood shake, slate, clay, cement or asbestos-cement tile, as well as over roofs that are water-soaked or badly deteriorated.

en.q: Per the IRC, what is the minimum slope for wood shingles?
en.e: Per the IRC (R905.7.1 for wood shingles and R905.8.1 for wood shakes), wood shingles and shakes need a slope of at least 3:12.

en.q: Per the IRC, what is the minimum slope for clay or concrete roof tile?
en.e: Per the IRC (R905.3.2), clay and concrete tile need a slope of at least 2-1/2:12. Slopes from 2-1/2:12 to less than 4:12 need double underlayment.

en.q: Per the IRC, what is the minimum slope for a built-up (tar and gravel) roof, other than coal-tar?
o: Flat (0:12)
1/8 inch per foot
1/4 inch per foot (1/4:12)
2 inches per foot (2:12)
en.e: Per the IRC (R905.9.1), built-up roofs need a design slope of at least 1/4 unit in 12 (2%) for drainage. Coal-tar built-up roofs may be 1/8:12.

en.q: Per the IRC, mineral-surfaced roll roofing must not be applied on slopes below:
en.e: Per the IRC (R905.5.2), mineral-surfaced roll roofing must not be applied on slopes below 1 unit vertical in 12 units horizontal.

en.q: Per the IRC, standing-seam metal roof systems may be installed down to a minimum slope of:
en.e: Per the IRC (R905.10.2), standing-seam metal roofs may go down to 1/4:12. Lapped, non-soldered seam metal roofs need 3:12, or 1/2:12 with applied lap sealant.

en.q: Per the IRC, where must drip edge be installed on an asphalt shingle roof?
o: Only along the eaves, where water drips off the roof edge into the gutters
Only along the rake (gable) edges, where wind-driven rain is the main concern
Along both the eaves and the rakes
Only where gutters are installed, because the gutter replaces the drip edge elsewhere
en.e: Per the IRC (R905.2.8.5), drip edge is required at eaves and rake edges of shingle roofs. Adjacent pieces overlap at least 2 inches, and the drip edge extends at least 1/4 inch below the roof sheathing.

en.q: Siding below the bottom end of a roof-to-wall intersection is stained and soft. There is no diverter flashing where the roof edge meets the wall. What flashing is missing?
o: Valley flashing
Counterflashing at the chimney
Kickout (diverter) flashing
Drip edge at the rake
en.e: Per the IRC (R903.2.1), a kickout (diverter) flashing is required where the eave of a roof meets a sidewall. Without it, water running down the step flashing flows into the wall instead of into the gutter.

en.q: Per the IRC, step flashing where a shingle roof meets a sidewall must be at least:
o: 2 inches high and 2 inches wide
4 inches high and 4 inches wide
6 inches high and 8 inches wide
10 inches high and 10 inches wide
en.e: Per the IRC (R905.2.8.3), base flashing against a vertical sidewall, whether continuous or step flashing, must be at least 4 inches high and 4 inches wide.

en.q: Under the IRC and typical manufacturer instructions, how many fasteners are normally required for each asphalt strip shingle on a typical-slope roof?
en.e: Per the IRC (R905.2.6), asphalt strip shingles need at least four fasteners each, or more where the manufacturer requires (for example, in high-wind areas or on very steep slopes).

en.q: Many shingles on a 22-year-old roof have bare patches where granules are gone, and lots of granules are collecting at the downspouts. What is the most likely explanation?
o: Hail damage from a storm within the past week or two
Normal aging, suggesting the roof is near the end of its life
Poor attic insulation that lets heat melt the granule adhesive
Installation over only a single layer of underlayment instead of two
en.e: Widespread, even granule loss on an older roof is a sign of aging. The inspector should report it and recommend that a roofer evaluate the roof, rather than predicting an exact remaining life.

en.q: Shingles on several slopes show randomly spaced dark spots where granules are missing, and the mat underneath feels soft when pressed. Metal roof vents have small dents. What is the most likely cause?
o: Hail impact
Foot traffic from installers
Manufacturing blisters
Algae growth
en.e: Random bruises with soft spots and dents in soft metals are typical signs of hail. The inspector should report possible storm damage and recommend evaluation by a roofer (the client may also want to contact the insurer).

en.q: After a windstorm, an inspector sees shingle tabs that are creased across the top, and a few tabs are missing. What is the most likely cause?
o: Hail
Ice damming
Wind lifting the tabs
Overheating from poor ventilation
en.e: Wind lifts and folds tabs, creasing them and breaking the seal, and can tear tabs off. Creased or missing tabs should be reported for repair.

en.q: Dark streaks run down the north slope of an asphalt shingle roof, but the shingles lie flat and are intact. What is the most likely cause, and how serious is it?
o: Rot in the roof deck; serious
Algae growth; mainly cosmetic
Hail damage; serious
Overheated shingles from poor attic ventilation; serious
en.e: Dark streaking on shady slopes is usually algae (often Gloeocapsa magma). It is mostly a cosmetic issue, unlike moss, which holds moisture and can lift shingles.

en.q: Thick moss is growing on a shaded asphalt shingle roof. Why should this be reported?
o: Moss makes the roof surface more fire-resistant and should be left alone
Moss holds moisture and can lift shingles, shortening roof life
Moss growth is a reliable sign that the roof was damaged by hail recently
Moss always means that the roof deck below it has rotted through completely
en.e: Moss retains water and its growth can lift shingle edges, allowing water entry and speeding wear. Removal by a roofer is commonly recommended.

en.q: The neoprene boot around a plumbing vent on the roof is cracked, and there is a water stain on the ceiling below it. What is the most likely source?
o: Condensation forming on the underside of the roof sheathing in the attic
A leaking water supply pipe running inside the wall next to the ceiling
Water entering through the cracked vent boot
A clogged gutter overflowing onto the soffit and running back into the ceiling
en.e: Rubber vent boots break down in sunlight over time. A cracked boot directly above a ceiling stain is the most likely leak source and should be replaced.

en.q: Nail heads are exposed through several shingles, and some have pushed up the shingle above them. What should the inspector recommend?
o: No action, because exposed nail heads are normal on most asphalt roofs
Repair by a roofer, because the nails can let water in
Painting the nail heads with roof paint so that they blend in with the shingles
Replacing the gutters, because nail pops are caused by overflowing gutters
en.e: Nail pops and exposed fasteners can let water past the shingles. They are a common, repairable defect that should be reported.

en.q: Shingle nails were placed well above the manufacturer's nailing line. What problem can this cause?
o: Reduced wind resistance and holding power
Too much granule loss from the shingle surface
Algae growth along the shingle tabs on shaded slopes
Ice damming at the eaves during the following winter
en.e: Manufacturers specify a nailing zone so that each nail goes through the overlap and holds two layers. High nailing reduces holding power and can lead to blow-offs.

en.q: A chimney has only roofing tar smeared around its base, with no step flashing or counterflashing, and the ceiling next to the chimney is stained. What should the inspector report?
o: That the tar is a permanent, acceptable flashing method if it is renewed every year
That proper flashing is missing and should be corrected by a roofer or mason
That the chimney must be removed down to below the roof line and rebuilt
That the ceiling stain is from condensation and is not related to the chimney at all
en.e: Roof cement alone is a temporary patch that cracks and fails. Chimneys need step (base) flashing plus counterflashing set into the masonry. The stain supports the conclusion that water is getting in.

en.q: Per the IRC, a cricket (saddle) is required on the upslope side of a chimney when the chimney's dimension parallel to the ridge is more than:
o: 12 inches
24 inches
30 inches
48 inches
en.e: Per the IRC (R1003.20 and R903.2.2), a cricket is required where the chimney dimension parallel to the ridge is greater than 30 inches, unless the chimney is at the ridge, to divert water and debris around it.

en.q: In the roofing industry, standing water on a low-slope roof is usually called "ponding" when it remains how long after rain?
o: More than 2 hours
More than 12 hours
More than 48 hours
More than 2 weeks
en.e: Industry practice (such as NRCA's) commonly calls water that remains more than 48 hours after rain, under conditions that allow drying, ponding. It speeds deterioration and points to poor drainage or sagging.

en.q: The surface of an older built-up roof shows a pattern of deep cracks that looks like reptile skin. What is this called, and what causes it?
o: Blistering, caused by moisture trapped between the plies of the roof
Alligatoring, from the asphalt aging in the sun
Fishmouthing, caused by poorly installed felt laps at the seams of the roof
Ridging, caused by movement of the roof deck under the membrane over time
en.e: Alligatoring is surface cracking of asphalt as it ages and becomes brittle from UV exposure. It shows the surfacing is worn out and needs maintenance or replacement.

en.q: On a modified bitumen roof, the inspector sees raised, soft bubbles in the membrane. What are these, and what is a common cause?
o: Fishmouths, caused by loose edge flashing lifting along the perimeter of the roof
Blisters, from trapped moisture or air that expands
Splits, caused by heavy foot traffic from service workers crossing the roof
Alligatoring, caused by sun damage that has dried out the membrane surface
en.e: Blisters are pockets where the membrane has separated, usually because moisture or air was trapped and expands with heat. They should be reported because they can rupture.

en.q: An EPDM (rubber) roof has seams that are peeling apart at the laps. What is the risk?
o: None, because EPDM membranes seal themselves at the laps over time
Water can enter at the open seams and leak inside
The roof will absorb more heat and become too hot in the summer months
The roof will become too heavy for the framing because of the loose sheets
en.e: EPDM is laid in sheets joined at seams with adhesive or tape. Open seams are a common leak point and should be repaired by a qualified roofer.

en.q: The roof is slate. Several slates are cracked and one has slipped out of place. How should the inspector inspect this roof?
o: From the ground, a ladder at the eaves, or a drone
By walking on the roof, as on any asphalt shingle roof of a similar slope
By removing a few slates to check the condition of the underlayment beneath
It should not be inspected at all, and the report should not mention the roof
en.e: Slate is brittle and easily broken underfoot. Inspectors usually view it from the ground, the eaves or a drone, and report the method used.

en.q: Under typical standards of practice, which statement about inspecting a roof is correct?
o: The inspector must walk on every roof, regardless of slope or weather
The inspector must certify in writing that the roof will not leak
The inspector need not walk the roof but must describe the method used
The inspector must estimate the roof's remaining life to the nearest year
en.e: Standards such as ASHI and InterNACHI let the inspector choose a safe method, such as walking, using binoculars or a drone, and require reporting the method used. They do not require walking the roof, certifying it or predicting remaining life.

en.q: It is raining, and the roof is a steep 12:12 slope with wet, slippery shingles. What is the most appropriate action?
o: Walk the roof carefully anyway, because the client paid for a full roof inspection
Skip the roof entirely and leave any mention of it out of the written report
Inspect from the ground, a ladder or a drone, and report the method and limits
Reschedule the whole inspection for the summer, when the roof will be dry and warm
en.e: Inspectors are not required to do anything unsafe. They should use another method and clearly state the method and its limits in the report.

en.q: Shingles on a 10-year-old roof are curling up at the edges (cupping) and down at the corners (clawing) across the whole roof. Which condition can speed this up?
o: A roof slope of 8:12, which is steeper than average
Poor attic ventilation that traps heat
Gutters that are too large for the size of the roof
Algae growing on the north-facing slopes of the roof
en.e: Curling is a sign of aging, and excess heat and moisture from an under-ventilated attic can speed it up. The inspector should report the curling and look for attic ventilation problems.

en.q: Viewed from the attic, the roof sheathing between rafters dips noticeably, and the roof felt spongy when walked on. What is the most likely condition?
o: Normal deflection that is found in all roof sheathing between rafters
Deteriorated or undersized roof sheathing
Framing that is too stiff, so the shingles cannot flex with the wind
An extra layer of shingles that makes the roof stronger and safer
en.e: Sagging sheathing and a spongy feel suggest delaminated, rotted or overspanned decking. The inspector should report it and recommend evaluation by a roofer or contractor.

en.q: Per the IRC, what is the basic required net free ventilating area for a vented attic?
o: 1/50 of the vented space
1/100 of the vented space
1/150 of the vented space
1/500 of the vented space
en.e: Per the IRC (R806.2), the minimum net free ventilating area is 1/150 of the area of the vented space, which may be reduced to 1/300 when the conditions in the exception are met.

en.q: Per the IRC, attic ventilation may be reduced from 1/150 to 1/300 when, among other options, at least 40% and no more than 50% of the required vent area is in the upper part of the attic. How far below the ridge may those upper vents be?
o: No more than 1 foot
No more than 3 feet
No more than 6 feet
Anywhere in the attic
en.e: Per the IRC (R806.2), the upper vents must be no more than 3 feet below the ridge or highest point of the space, measured vertically, with the rest of the required ventilation at the eaves or cornice.

en.q: An attic has 1,500 square feet of vented space. Per the IRC basic 1/150 ratio, how much net free ventilating area is required?
o: 5 square feet
10 square feet
15 square feet
150 square feet
en.e: 1,500 divided by 150 equals 10 square feet of net free area. If the 1/300 exception applies, the requirement would be 5 square feet.

en.q: Per the IRC, openings in attic ventilation covers (screens) must be at least 1/16 inch and no more than:
o: 1/8 inch
1/4 inch
1/2 inch
1 inch
en.e: Per the IRC (R806.1), ventilation openings must have corrosion-resistant mesh or similar covers with openings between 1/16 inch and 1/4 inch, which keeps out animals but still lets air flow.

en.q: Per the IRC, where insulation could block eave vents, a baffle must keep an air space of at least how much between the insulation and the roof sheathing at the vent?
o: 1 inch
1/4 inch
3 inches
6 inches
en.e: Per the IRC (R806.3), where eave or cornice vents are installed, insulation must not block free airflow, and a minimum 1-inch space must be kept between the insulation and the roof sheathing at the vent.

en.q: In winter, thick ice builds up along the eaves, and water stains show up on the ceiling near exterior walls. What is the usual root cause?
o: Gutters that are too large for the roof, so they fill with snow
Attic heat melting snow that refreezes at the cold eaves
Shingles installed with too many nails, which conduct cold into the roof
A roof slope that is too steep, so snow slides down and piles up at the eaves
en.e: Ice dams form when warm attic surfaces melt snow that refreezes at the cold overhang. Air sealing, insulation and ventilation are the long-term fixes; an ice barrier limits leaks.

en.q: In the attic, the inspector finds frost and dark staining on the sheathing right above a bathroom exhaust fan that has no duct. What is the most appropriate recommendation?
o: Add more insulation on top of the fan housing to stop the condensation
Have the fan ducted to the exterior
Turn the fan off permanently and rely on opening the bathroom door instead
Install a second fan in the attic to blow the moist air out the gable vent
en.e: Per the IRC (M1501.1), exhaust air must go to the outdoors, not into the attic. Warm, moist air from the bathroom condenses on cold sheathing and causes mold and decay.

en.q: How can an inspector usually estimate how many layers of shingles are on a roof without removing any?
o: By weighing a single shingle removed from the field of the roof
By measuring the attic temperature on a sunny afternoon
By looking at the roof edges and penetrations
By counting the number of nails used in one shingle
en.e: Layers can often be counted where the roof edges are visible, at drip edges, rakes or around vents. This is a non-destructive way to estimate the number of roof coverings.

en.q: The first course of shingles at the eave has no starter strip, so water can run through the tab cutouts onto the sheathing. What is the best report entry?
o: Acceptable, because starter strips are an optional upgrade on shingle roofs
Improper installation; recommend repair by a qualified roofer
The gutters should be removed so that water can drain freely off the eave
More attic insulation should be installed to keep the eave from leaking
en.e: Manufacturers require a starter course so that the gaps between the first course's tabs are covered and the first course is sealed down. Without it, water and wind can get under the first course.

en.q: A gutter is full of debris and overflowing, and the fascia behind it is rotted. What should the inspector recommend?
o: Cleaning, fascia repair and routine gutter maintenance
Adding a second downspout at the other end while leaving the debris in place
Painting the gutters and fascia with a water-resistant exterior coating
Filling the low spots in the gutter with sealant so that water flows faster
en.e: Clogged gutters overflow behind the gutter, rot the fascia and send water to the foundation. Cleaning, repairing the damage and routine maintenance solve the problem.

en.q: On a concrete tile roof, what usually provides the main waterproofing?
o: The tiles alone
The underlayment beneath the tiles
The paint on the tiles
The battens that hold the tiles
en.e: Tiles shed most water, but water gets past the joints, so the underlayment is the main waterproofing layer. Old underlayment often fails before the tiles do.

en.q: What is a closed-cut valley?
o: A valley lined with exposed metal, where no shingles cross the valley center
One slope's shingles run through the valley; the other slope's are cut along a line
A valley where the shingles from both slopes are interlaced (woven) together
A valley that is sealed with roof tar and is left without any shingles at all
en.e: In a closed-cut valley, one slope's shingles run through the valley and the other slope's shingles are trimmed along a line. Open valleys show metal; woven valleys interlace both slopes.

en.q: A satellite dish has been bolted directly through the shingles in the middle of a roof slope, with no flashing. What is the concern?
o: The dish may lower the roof temperature
The fastener holes can let water into the roof
Satellite dishes attract lightning
The dish voids the house's electrical service
en.e: Penetrations through roofing need proper flashing or sealing. Bolts through shingles are a common leak source; the dish itself is outside the inspection, but its effect on the roof is not.

en.q: A skylight has water stains on the drywall around its interior shaft. What should the inspector do?
o: Report the stains and recommend evaluation of the skylight by a roofer
State that all skylights eventually leak and that this one must be removed
Say nothing, because skylights are excluded from every standard of practice
Recommend painting over the stain with stain-blocking primer and moving on
en.e: Skylights are a frequent leak point at the curb flashing or the glazing seals. The inspector should report the evidence; a moisture meter can show whether the area is wet at the time of inspection.

en.q: Why might new asphalt shingles installed in cold weather not seal down properly?
o: The roofing nails contract and rust in cold weather, loosening the shingles
The sealant strips need heat to bond
The shingles shrink permanently in the cold, so the courses no longer overlap
The granules fall off in cold weather, which prevents the shingles from sealing
en.e: Self-sealing strips are activated by heat. In cold weather, shingles may stay unsealed and vulnerable to wind until temperatures rise, unless hand-sealed per the manufacturer.

en.q: Under typical standards of practice, which of these is the inspector NOT required to do when inspecting a roof?
o: Inspect flashings around roof penetrations
Inspect the roof covering
Report the method used to inspect the roof
Remove snow or ice to see the roof surface
en.e: Typical standards of practice require inspecting the roof covering, flashings, gutters and penetrations and describing the method used. They do not require removing snow, ice or debris, which is a limitation to report.

en.q: A low-slope roof has a single interior drain, and the area around it holds water. What additional feature is commonly needed so that the roof can drain if that drain clogs?
o: A larger gutter along the edge of the roof
A secondary (overflow) drain or scupper
A thicker roof membrane over the whole roof
More insulation below the roof deck
en.e: Roofs that drain to interior drains or are surrounded by parapets need secondary drains or scuppers so that a clogged primary drain does not cause dangerous ponding or leaks.

en.q: Per the IRC, the bottom of an exterior footing must be at least how far below the surface of undisturbed ground, regardless of frost depth?
o: 6 inches
12 inches
24 inches
36 inches
en.e: Per the IRC (R403.1.4), exterior footings must be at least 12 inches below undisturbed ground and also below the frost line set by the local jurisdiction, unless frost-protected by another approved method.

en.q: Per the IRC, what are the minimum diameter and maximum spacing of anchor bolts that fasten a wood sill plate to a foundation?
o: 3/8 inch, 8 feet on center
1/2 inch, 6 feet on center
5/8 inch, 10 feet on center
1/4 inch, 4 feet on center
en.e: Per the IRC (R403.1.6), anchor bolts must be at least 1/2 inch in diameter, spaced no more than 6 feet apart, embedded at least 7 inches, with a bolt within 12 inches of each end of each plate section.

en.q: Per the IRC, an anchor bolt must be located within how far of each end of each sill plate section?
o: 4 inches
12 inches
24 inches
36 inches
en.e: Per the IRC (R403.1.6), there must be at least two bolts per plate section, with one bolt within 12 inches of each end of each section.

en.q: A concrete block basement wall has a long horizontal crack about halfway up, and the wall bows inward along the crack. What is the most likely cause, and what should the inspector recommend?
o: Normal concrete shrinkage; no action is needed beyond sealing the crack
Lateral soil and water pressure; refer to a structural engineer
A roof leak running down inside the wall; repair the roof flashing first
Frost forming in the attic and loading the walls; add attic insulation
en.e: A horizontal crack with inward bowing in a block wall is a classic sign of lateral pressure from soil and water. It can get worse and is a significant structural concern that needs an engineer.

en.q: A brick or concrete block wall shows a crack that zigzags along the mortar joints in a stair-step pattern. What does this usually indicate?
o: Differential settlement or movement of the foundation
Shrinkage of poured concrete as it cures
Termite activity in the mortar
Too much insulation in the wall
en.e: Stair-step cracking through mortar joints usually shows that one part of the wall moved relative to another, often from settlement. Width, displacement and signs of ongoing movement determine how serious it is.

en.q: A poured concrete basement wall has a single narrow vertical crack with no displacement and no water entry. What is the most likely cause?
o: Lateral soil pressure pushing the wall inward
Shrinkage as the concrete cured
An overloaded roof bearing down on the wall
Frost heave lifting the footing in winter
en.e: Narrow vertical cracks in poured walls are typically from shrinkage and are usually not structurally significant. They can still let water in, and wide, displaced or growing cracks need further evaluation.

en.q: Interior drywall shows diagonal cracks running up from the corners of several doors and windows, and some doors stick. What is the most likely explanation?
o: Paint that was applied too thickly over the joints
Structural movement, such as settlement
High-quality drywall finishing that is too rigid
A plumbing leak in the attic running down the walls
en.e: Openings are weak points where movement shows up as diagonal cracks and doors that bind. The inspector should report the pattern and look for its cause in the foundation and framing.

en.q: Bricks on a chimney and on the lower part of a wall have faces that are flaking off (spalling). What usually causes this?
o: Termites tunneling through the brick faces
Absorbed water freezing and thawing
Too much mortar packed into the joints
Lightning strikes on the chimney over time
en.e: Spalling happens when absorbed water freezes and expands, breaking off the brick face. It indicates excess moisture, such as from missing caps, poor drainage or hard, impermeable mortar.

en.q: Per the IRC, notches in the top or bottom of solid sawn floor joists must not exceed what fraction of the joist depth, and must not be in which part of the span?
o: 1/3 of the depth; the outer third
1/4 of the depth; the end sixth
1/6 of the depth; the middle third
1/2 of the depth; the middle sixth
en.e: Per the IRC (R502.8.1), notches in solid lumber joists must not exceed 1/6 of the depth, must not be longer than 1/3 of the depth, and must not be in the middle third of the span. Notches at the ends must not exceed 1/4 of the depth.

en.q: Per the IRC, bored holes in solid sawn floor joists must not be within how far of the top or bottom edge, and must not exceed what diameter?
o: 1/2 inch of the edge; 1/2 of the joist depth
1 inch of the edge; 1/4 of the joist depth
2 inches of the edge; 1/3 of the joist depth
3 inches of the edge; 2/3 of the joist depth
en.e: Per the IRC (R502.8.1), holes in solid joists must be no closer than 2 inches to the top or bottom and no larger than 1/3 of the joist depth.

en.q: In a crawl space, the inspector sees that a floor joist has been notched several inches deep on the bottom edge near mid-span to fit a drain pipe. How should this be reported?
o: As acceptable, because the drain pipe needed the space to slope properly
As a structural defect needing repair by a contractor or engineer
As a cosmetic issue, because the notch is hidden in the crawl space
As a plumbing defect only, to be corrected by moving the drain pipe later
en.e: A deep notch on the bottom (tension) edge in the middle third of the span greatly weakens a joist and is not allowed by the IRC. It should be reported for repair, such as sistering or a header.

en.q: Per the IRC, in an exterior or bearing wall, a stud may be bored with a hole no larger than what percentage of its width, unless it is doubled?
o: 25 percent
40 percent
60 percent
75 percent
en.e: Per the IRC (R602.6), bored holes in bearing-wall studs may be up to 40% of the stud width, or up to 60% if the stud is doubled and no more than two successive studs are bored. Notches are limited to 25%.

en.q: Per the IRC, in a bearing wall, a stud may be notched no more than what percentage of its width?
o: 25 percent
40 percent
50 percent
60 percent
en.e: Per the IRC (R602.6), studs in exterior or bearing walls may be notched up to 25% of their width. Nonbearing partition studs may be notched up to 40%.

en.q: Per the IRC, when a pipe cuts through more than 50% of the width of a top plate, what is required?
o: Nothing, as long as the cut is in a wall that carries a roof load
Filling the hole around the pipe with fire-rated spray foam only
A metal strap across the cut, fastened on each side
Replacing the whole top plate along the length of the wall
en.e: Per the IRC (R602.6.1), where piping or ductwork cuts more than 50% of a top plate's width in an exterior or bearing wall, a galvanized metal strap must be fastened across and to the plate on each side of the opening.

en.q: In the attic, the inspector finds that a web member of a manufactured roof truss has been cut to make room for an air handler. What is the most appropriate action?
o: Report it as acceptable as long as the cut is clean and square
Nail a short board beside the cut, then continue the inspection without comment
Report it as a defect and refer it to an engineer or the truss manufacturer
Recommend adding insulation around the cut to protect the truss from moisture
en.e: Trusses are engineered systems; cutting or altering any member can compromise the whole truss. Repairs require a design from an engineer or the truss manufacturer.

en.q: The bottom flange of an I-joist has been notched to fit a duct. What is the concern?
o: The flange must not be cut, so the joist may be seriously weakened
None, because I-joists are much stronger than solid lumber joists
Only a cosmetic concern, because the flange is hidden by the ceiling
The duct will be too small for the airflow needed by the room above
en.e: Manufacturers prohibit cutting or notching I-joist flanges. Only holes in the web are allowed, at the sizes and locations the manufacturer specifies. A cut flange is a structural defect.

en.q: What is the main structural purpose of rafter ties (or ceiling joists tied to the rafters) in a conventionally framed gable roof?
o: To support attic storage
To resist the rafters' outward thrust on the walls
To provide nailing for the ceiling drywall only
To hold down the roof against wind uplift
en.e: Rafter ties connect the rafter ends to keep the walls from spreading apart under the roof load. Collar ties in the upper third of the attic mainly resist wind uplift and ridge separation.

en.q: The ridge of a stick-framed roof sags, and the top of the exterior walls leans outward. There are no ceiling joists or rafter ties connecting the rafters. What is the likely cause?
o: Hail damage that has cracked the roof sheathing
Rafter thrust spreading the walls
Normal settling of a newly built roof
Too much attic ventilation drying out the rafters
en.e: Without rafter ties or a structural ridge beam, rafters push the walls outward and the ridge drops. This is a significant structural defect that needs an engineer or contractor.

en.q: Per the IRC, when the roof slope is less than 3:12, the member at the ridge that supports the rafters must be:
o: A 1-inch ridge board
A collar tie
Designed as a beam
Omitted
en.e: Per the IRC (R802.3), where the roof pitch is less than 3:12, the members that support rafters (such as the ridge) must be designed as beams, because the rafters create little thrust that ceiling joists can resist.

en.q: Per the IRC, in a crawl space, wood joists closer than how far to exposed ground must be naturally durable or preservative-treated?
o: 6 inches
12 inches
18 inches
24 inches
en.e: Per the IRC (R317.1), wood joists or the bottom of a wood structural floor less than 18 inches from exposed ground, and wood girders less than 12 inches from exposed ground, must be decay-resistant.

en.q: Per the IRC, wood girders in a crawl space closer than how far to exposed ground must be naturally durable or preservative-treated?
o: 6 inches
12 inches
18 inches
24 inches
en.e: Per the IRC (R317.1), girders closer than 12 inches to exposed ground in a crawl space must be decay-resistant. The limit for joists is 18 inches.

en.q: Per the IRC, what is the minimum size of an access opening through a floor into a crawl space?
o: 12 by 18 inches
18 by 24 inches
22 by 30 inches
24 by 36 inches
en.e: Per the IRC (R408.4), a crawl space access opening through the floor must be at least 18 by 24 inches; an opening through a perimeter wall must be at least 16 by 24 inches.

en.q: Per the IRC, for a vented crawl space with no ground vapor retarder, what is the minimum net vent area?
o: 1 square foot for each 50 square feet of crawl space
1 square foot for each 150 square feet of crawl space
1 square foot for each 300 square feet of crawl space
1 square foot for each 1,500 square feet of crawl space
en.e: Per the IRC (R408.1), vented crawl spaces need 1 square foot of net vent area for each 150 square feet of crawl space. The area may be reduced to 1/1,500 when the ground is covered with a Class I vapor retarder.

en.q: Per the IRC, crawl space foundation vents should be placed so that one is within how far of each corner of the building?
o: 1 foot
3 feet
6 feet
10 feet
en.e: Per the IRC (R408.1), one ventilation opening must be within 3 feet of each corner of the building to provide cross ventilation.

en.q: A crawl space floor is bare soil with no vapor retarder, and the wood framing has high moisture readings and visible fungal growth. What is the most appropriate recommendation?
o: Seal all the foundation vents tightly and take no other action
Refer to a contractor for moisture control, such as a ground cover
Recommend insulating the crawl space walls only, without other changes
Make no comment, because crawl spaces are expected to be damp
en.e: Exposed soil releases moisture that raises wood moisture content and supports decay and fungal growth. A ground cover plus correction of drainage and ventilation addresses the source.

en.q: The inspector sees pencil-width mud tubes running up a foundation wall to the wood sill. What is the most appropriate action?
o: Break the tubes and report that the termites are gone
Report it and refer to a licensed pest professional
Spray insecticide on the tubes and the sill plate
Ignore it, because insects are outside every inspection
en.e: Mud tubes are a sign of subterranean termites. Typical standards of practice do not require the inspector to identify pests, but reporting visible evidence and referring to a licensed specialist is appropriate.

en.q: Small piles of coarse sawdust containing insect parts are found beneath a wood window frame. Which insect is most likely responsible?
o: Subterranean termites
Carpenter ants
Powderpost beetles
Drywood termites
en.e: Carpenter ants excavate wood to nest but do not eat it, pushing out coarse frass that often contains insect parts. Powderpost beetles leave a fine, flour-like powder and tiny exit holes.

en.q: Wood joists show many tiny round holes with a fine, flour-like powder below them. Which pest is most likely?
o: Carpenter ants
Subterranean termites
Powderpost beetles
Carpenter bees
en.e: Powderpost beetle larvae tunnel through wood and leave small round exit holes and fine powder. Carpenter bees make larger, perfectly round entry holes in exposed wood surfaces.

en.q: Decayed wood shows dark, crumbly pieces that break into small cube-shaped chunks. What type of decay is this?
o: Brown rot
White rot
Soft rot from surface mold only
Fire damage
en.e: Brown rot attacks cellulose and leaves wood dark and cracked into cubes. All wood decay needs sustained moisture, so the source of water should be identified.

en.q: A garage slab is stamped as a post-tensioned slab. What should the inspector advise the client?
o: That the slab can be cut or drilled anywhere without special precautions
That it must not be cut or drilled without professional guidance
That post-tensioned slabs are prohibited in residential construction
That the stamp means the slab has failed and needs to be replaced
en.e: Post-tensioned slabs contain high-tension steel tendons. Cutting or drilling into one can cause injury and damage the slab, so any work must be planned by qualified professionals.

en.q: In a basement, a beam is supported by a telescoping screw-jack post that looks like a temporary shoring post, sitting on the slab with no visible footing. What should the inspector report?
o: That the support is a permanent, approved installation that needs no comment
That it appears temporary and should be evaluated by a professional
That the client should tighten the jack a few turns to level the floor above
Nothing, because posts in basements are not part of the structure
en.e: Temporary jack posts are not intended as permanent supports, and posts need adequate footings. The inspector should report it and refer it to a qualified professional.

en.q: Per the IRC, the ends of floor joists must bear at least how far on masonry or concrete?
o: 1 inch
1-1/2 inches
3 inches
6 inches
en.e: Per the IRC (R502.6), joist ends must bear at least 1-1/2 inches on wood or metal and at least 3 inches on masonry or concrete (unless supported by approved hangers).

en.q: Floors throughout a home feel noticeably bouncy and sag slightly at mid-span. What is a likely cause?
o: Too much insulation between the floor joists
Undersized, overspanned or weakened joists
Hardwood flooring installed over the subfloor
A new roof adding weight to the exterior walls
en.e: Excess deflection usually comes from joists that are too small for the span or weakened. The inspector should report it and recommend evaluation, not calculate spans.

en.q: Above a garage door in a brick veneer wall, a horizontal crack runs along the opening, and the steel lintel is heavily rusted and has expanded. What is happening?
o: Normal settlement of the brick over a wide opening
Rust jacking from the corroding lintel
Frost heave of the garage slab lifting the door frame
A roof leak through the attic running down the wall
en.e: Rusting steel expands and can lift and crack the brick above it. A mason or contractor should evaluate the lintel and the masonry.

en.q: In late winter, cracks appear where interior partition walls meet the ceiling, and they close again in summer. The roof is framed with trusses. What is the most likely cause?
o: Truss uplift
Foundation settlement at the center of the house
Undersized floor joists sagging between bearing walls
A leaking water heater wetting the wall framing
en.e: Truss uplift is seasonal. Bottom chords buried in cold, damp attic insulation and top chords in the warm, dry attic expand and contract differently. It is usually not a structural defect but can be reported and explained.

en.q: Several small nail heads have pushed out through the drywall in a newer home, creating round bumps. What is the most likely cause?
o: Termites eating the framing behind the drywall
Framing shrinking as it dries
Foundation failure lifting the walls
An electrical short heating the nails
en.e: Nail pops typically result from the framing drying and shrinking after construction. They are usually cosmetic.

en.q: A basement wall shows a horizontal line of staining at the same height all around the room, plus efflorescence below the line. What is the most likely explanation?
o: A leaking pipe running along one of the walls
Past flooding up to that level
Normal condensation on the cool basement walls
Paint that was applied in two different colors
en.e: A consistent "tide line" suggests water stood in the basement at that level. The inspector should report the evidence and recommend asking the seller about its history and evaluating drainage.

en.q: Steel wall anchor plates appear on the inside of a basement wall at regular intervals. What do these usually indicate?
o: A past repair of a moving wall
A decorative feature added to the wall
New anchor bolts for the sill plate above
A plumbing cleanout for the floor drain
en.e: Wall anchors or braces show that the wall has moved in the past. The inspector should report them and recommend obtaining documentation, such as an engineer's report and warranty, and checking for ongoing movement.

en.q: What is the main structural concern with an older stone (rubble) foundation whose mortar has become soft and sandy?
o: The stones will absorb too much heat in summer and crack
The wall is weakened and can let water and pests in
Sandy mortar makes the wall too heavy for its footing
Rubble foundations cannot be repointed, so they must be replaced
en.e: Deteriorated mortar reduces the wall's strength and stability and allows water and pest entry. Repointing by a qualified mason is a common recommendation.

en.q: Expansive clay soils are associated with which kind of foundation problem?
o: Rapid rusting of the anchor bolts in the sill plate
Heaving and settling as the soil swells and shrinks
Excessive radon entry with no other effect on the house
Wood rot in the attic caused by soil moisture rising
en.e: Expansive clays change volume with moisture. Foundations can heave or settle, causing cracks and uneven floors. Steady moisture levels and good drainage help.

en.q: The bottom plate of a finished basement wall sits directly on the concrete slab. Per the IRC, what type of wood should it be?
o: Any untreated softwood, as long as it is kiln-dried
Preservative-treated or naturally durable wood
Hardwood only, because softwoods absorb moisture
Engineered I-joist material laid flat on the slab
en.e: Per the IRC (R317.1), wood sills and sleepers on concrete that is in direct contact with the ground, and wood framing on concrete or masonry that is near exposed ground, must be decay-resistant.

en.q: A window header in a bearing wall is visibly sagging, and the window no longer opens. What is the most likely cause?
o: High humidity in the room swelling the window sash
An undersized or missing header
A worn window lock that no longer releases the sash
Too much caulk applied around the window frame
en.e: A header carries load across an opening. If it is undersized, missing or overloaded, it sags and can rack the window. This should be reported for evaluation by a contractor or engineer.

en.q: An inspector finds a long, wide crack in a foundation wall with one side offset from the other by about 1/2 inch. Which recommendation is most appropriate?
o: Fill the crack with caulk and monitor it for changes
Refer it to a structural engineer
Report it as typical concrete shrinkage
Recommend replacing the entire foundation now
en.e: Displacement across a crack shows structural movement beyond normal shrinkage. The inspector should not diagnose the cause or design a repair, but should refer it to an engineer.

en.q: Per the IRC, a ground vapor retarder in a crawl space should have its joints lapped by at least how much?
o: 1 inch
6 inches
12 inches
24 inches
en.e: Per the IRC (R408.3), the Class I vapor retarder in an unvented crawl space must have joints overlapped by 6 inches and sealed or taped, with edges extending at least 6 inches up the stem wall.

en.q: What is the main purpose of sistering a floor joist?
o: To lower the floor height in the room above
To strengthen a weak or damaged joist
To add insulation between the floor joists
To make room for plumbing drains in the floor
en.e: Sistering means attaching a full or partial-length new member beside a damaged joist so that both carry the load. It is a common repair for cracked, notched or decayed joists.

en.q: Under typical standards of practice, which of these is the home inspector NOT required to do when inspecting the structure?
o: Describe the foundation type
Report signs of significant movement
Probe structural components where deterioration is suspected
Calculate the strength or adequacy of structural members
en.e: Inspectors describe and inspect visible structure and report deficiencies, but engineering calculations of strength, adequacy and span are excluded from standards of practice.

en.q: In a crawl space, the inspector finds wood form boards left in contact with soil under the floor framing. Why should this be reported?
o: Form boards are required by code to stay in place under the floor
Wood debris on soil attracts termites and decay
Form boards improve cross ventilation in the crawl space
The boards make the crawl space easier for workers to enter
en.e: Cellulose debris left in crawl spaces, especially in contact with soil, invites termites and fungi. Removing it is a common recommendation.

en.q: A brick veneer wall is bulging outward between floors, and the mortar joints near the bulge are cracked. What is the most likely concern?
o: Normal thermal expansion of brick on sunny walls
Failed or missing veneer ties, or hidden moisture damage
Good, flexible mortar that allows the wall to move
An overloaded floor inside pressing on the wall
en.e: Veneer depends on metal ties to the structure behind it. Bulging suggests failed ties or hidden damage, which is a potential safety hazard; a mason or engineer should evaluate it.

en.q: When inspecting a basement with finished walls and ceilings, what limitation should the inspector report?
o: That the structure is free of defects because the finishes are in good condition
That finishes concealed the structure, limiting the inspection
That finished basements are built to a higher standard and never have defects
That the inspector removed wall panels to look behind them where possible
en.e: Inspectors report on readily accessible, visible components. Finished surfaces conceal structure, and the report should clearly state that limitation.

en.q: A support column in a basement is leaning, and its base is not centered on its footing. What should the inspector do?
o: Straighten the column by tapping its base back into place with a hammer
Report it and refer it to a qualified contractor or engineer
Report it as acceptable, as long as the floor above it appears to be level
Recommend painting the column with rust-inhibiting paint to protect it
en.e: A leaning or displaced column may not carry its load properly. The inspector should report it and refer it rather than attempting adjustments or judging it safe.

en.q: Per the IRC, when the static water pressure entering a house exceeds what value is a pressure-reducing valve required?
o: 40 psi
60 psi
80 psi
150 psi
en.e: Per the IRC (P2903.3.1), maximum static pressure is 80 psi. Where the street pressure is higher, an approved pressure-reducing valve is required.

en.q: An inspector screws a pressure gauge onto an exterior hose bibb and reads 110 psi. What is the most appropriate recommendation?
o: Have a licensed plumber install or adjust a pressure-reducing valve
No action, because higher pressure gives better showers
Replace all faucets with low-flow models
Turn the main shut-off valve partly closed
en.e: Pressure above 80 psi strains fixtures, valves and water heaters and causes leaks. A properly adjusted pressure-reducing valve is the accepted fix; throttling the main valve is not a proper correction.

en.q: Per the IRC, what is the minimum static water pressure at the building entrance for a water service?
o: 15 psi
40 psi
60 psi
80 psi
en.e: Per the IRC (P2903.3), static pressure at the building entrance must be at least 40 psi. Where it is lower, a booster system may be needed.

en.q: When the inspector opens the bathroom sink faucet, the flow in the tub on the same floor drops to a trickle. The house has original galvanized steel supply pipes. What is the most likely cause?
o: A water heater that is too large for the house
Corrosion and scale inside the old galvanized pipes
A missing vent on the drain system serving the tub
High water pressure coming in from the city main
en.e: Galvanized steel corrodes and scales internally with age, narrowing the pipe. Running two fixtures at once (functional flow) shows the restriction. A plumber should evaluate the system.

en.q: Gray plastic water supply piping with crimp rings is found in a house built in 1988. What is the most likely material, and what is the concern?
o: PEX; there is no particular concern
CPVC; it is too heavy for the framing
Polybutylene; it is prone to failure
Copper; it corrodes quickly in most water
en.e: Polybutylene, used roughly from the late 1970s to the mid-1990s, is prone to failure, especially at fittings, and was the subject of large class-action suits. The inspector should identify it and recommend evaluation by a plumber.

en.q: Under federal law, lead solder was banned for use in potable water systems beginning in:
en.e: The 1986 amendments to the Safe Drinking Water Act banned lead pipe and lead solder (over 0.2% lead) in potable water systems. Homes plumbed with copper before then may have lead-bearing solder.

en.q: A copper water pipe is connected directly to a galvanized steel pipe with no fitting between them, and the joint is heavily corroded. What is the cause?
o: Hard water depositing minerals at the joint
High water temperature softening the joint
Galvanic corrosion between dissimilar metals
Too little water pressure in the supply line
en.e: Joining dissimilar metals in water creates galvanic corrosion at the connection. A dielectric fitting (or other approved transition) is used to separate them.

en.q: Per the IRC, what is the minimum slope for a horizontal drain pipe 2-1/2 inches in diameter or smaller?
o: 1/16 inch per foot
1/8 inch per foot
1/4 inch per foot
1/2 inch per foot
en.e: Per the IRC (P3005.3), horizontal drainage pipe 2-1/2 inches or smaller needs 1/4 inch per foot; 3 to 6 inches needs 1/8 inch per foot.

en.q: Per the IRC, what is the minimum slope for a 4-inch horizontal building drain?
o: 1/16 inch per foot
1/8 inch per foot
1/4 inch per foot
1/2 inch per foot
en.e: Per the IRC (Table P3005.3), drain pipe 3 inches through 6 inches in diameter needs a slope of at least 1/8 inch per foot.

en.q: Per the IRC, the liquid seal in a fixture trap must be at least ___ and no more than ___ deep.
o: 1 inch; 2 inches
2 inches; 4 inches
3 inches; 6 inches
4 inches; 8 inches
en.e: Per the IRC (P3201.2), each fixture trap must have a liquid seal of not less than 2 inches and not more than 4 inches (with a deeper seal allowed for floor drains and similar traps where evaporation is a concern).

en.q: Under a bathroom sink, the drain makes an "S" shape that drops straight down into the floor with no vent connection. What is the concern?
o: The trap holds too much water and drains slowly
The trap can siphon dry, letting sewer gas in
S-traps cause high water pressure in the supply
S-traps are required on all lavatory sinks
