en.e: S-traps are prohibited by the IRC (P3201.5) because the falling water can siphon the trap dry. A P-trap with a proper vent connection is the accepted configuration.

en.q: A sink drain uses a flexible, corrugated (accordion-style) plastic pipe as the trap. Why should this be reported?
o: It is more expensive than a standard trap and adapter
Traps need a smooth interior; corrugated pipe clogs
Corrugated traps are permitted only for kitchen sinks
It makes the hot water in the sink too hot to use
en.e: Per the IRC (P3201.2 and P3201.5), traps must have a smooth, uniform interior. Corrugated flexible pipe traps debris and is not an approved trap.

en.q: Per the IRC, an open vent pipe through a roof must extend at least how far above the roof?
o: 2 inches
6 inches
12 inches
24 inches
en.e: Per the IRC (P3103.1), open vent pipes must terminate at least 6 inches above the roof (higher where the roof is used for other purposes or where local snow depth requires).

en.q: Per the IRC, a plumbing vent terminal near an openable window must be at least 10 feet away horizontally unless it is at least how far above the top of the window?
o: 1 foot
2 feet
3 feet
6 feet
en.e: Per the IRC (P3103.5), vent terminals must be at least 4 feet below, 10 feet horizontally from, or 3 feet above any door, openable window or other air intake within 10 feet, to keep sewer gas out.

en.q: When a bathtub drains, the nearby bathroom sink drain gurgles. What is the most likely cause?
o: A venting problem
A water heater that is too small for the house
Too much water pressure in the supply lines
A loose toilet seat letting air into the drain
en.e: Gurgling usually means air is being pulled through a trap because of poor venting or a partial blockage. The trap seal can be siphoned, so a plumber should evaluate it.

en.q: Which statement about the temperature and pressure relief (TPR) valve discharge pipe is correct per the IRC?
o: It should be reduced to 1/2 inch so that the discharge comes out more slowly
It should have a shut-off valve so that it can be closed during repairs
It must be full size, drain by gravity, and have no valves or end threads
It should rise up through the attic and out through the roof to the outdoors
en.e: Per the IRC (P2804.6.1), the discharge pipe must not be smaller than the valve outlet, must not have valves or tees, must drain by gravity, and must not be threaded at its end, so that it cannot be capped.

en.q: Per the IRC, a TPR valve discharge pipe that ends near the floor should terminate no more than how far above the floor or waste receptor?
o: 2 inches
6 inches
12 inches
24 inches
en.e: Per the IRC (P2804.6.1), the discharge must end no more than 6 inches above the floor or the flood-level rim of the waste receptor (and no less than two pipe diameters above it), so that scalding water is directed downward.

en.q: A water heater's TPR valve discharge pipe has a threaded cap screwed onto its end. What is the most appropriate report comment?
o: Acceptable, because the cap keeps the floor dry when the valve weeps
A serious hazard, because the cap blocks the relief path
A cosmetic issue to be handled when the water heater is replaced
Acceptable as long as the water heater is less than five years old
en.e: A capped discharge pipe defeats the safety valve and can allow a water heater to explode if it overheats. That is why the IRC prohibits threads at the outlet end.

en.q: Why do most standards of practice say an inspector is not required to operate the TPR valve on a water heater?
o: The valve can only be tested with special tools that inspectors do not carry
It may discharge scalding water or fail to reseat
It is illegal for anyone other than a licensed plumber to touch a TPR valve
The valve is normally hidden inside the tank and cannot be reached
en.e: Typical standards of practice exclude operating safety valves. A TPR valve that has not opened in years may not reseat, creating a leak, and the discharge is scalding hot.

en.q: Per the IRC, in a garage, a fuel-fired water heater with an ignition source must have the ignition source at least how high above the floor, unless the appliance is listed as flammable-vapor-ignition-resistant?
o: 6 inches
12 inches
18 inches
36 inches
en.e: Per the IRC (M1307.3 and G2408.2), appliances with an ignition source in a garage must be elevated so that the ignition source is at least 18 inches above the floor, because gasoline vapors are heavier than air. FVIR-listed water heaters are exempt.

en.q: A gas water heater in a garage sits in the path of the car, with no barrier in front of it. Per the IRC, what is needed?
o: Protection from vehicle impact
Nothing, because water heaters are designed to resist impacts from vehicles
A larger gas supply line so that the heater can recover more quickly
A thermal expansion tank mounted on the cold water line above the heater
en.e: Per the IRC (M1307.3.1 and G2408.3), appliances in garages must be protected from motor vehicle impact.

en.q: Per the IRC, where seismic strapping of a water heater is required, the straps must be in which locations?
o: One strap at the very top of the tank only, anchored to the ceiling
In the upper and lower thirds of the tank
Wrapped around the gas line and the water lines above the tank
At mid-height only, with one strap fastened to each side wall
en.e: Per the IRC (P2801.8), in Seismic Design Categories D0, D1 and D2 (and for townhouses in C), water heaters must be anchored or strapped in the upper third and lower third of the tank, with the lower strap at least 4 inches above the controls.

en.q: Per the IRC, where a water heater is installed where a leak would cause damage, it must have a drain pan at least how deep, with what minimum drain size?
o: 1/2 inch deep; 1/2-inch drain
1-1/2 inches deep; 3/4-inch drain
3 inches deep; 1-inch drain
6 inches deep; 2-inch drain
en.e: Per the IRC (P2801.6), the pan must be at least 1-1/2 inches deep and drain through a pipe at least 3/4 inch in diameter to an approved location.

en.q: A house has a backflow preventer (check valve) on the water service, creating a closed system. Per the IRC, what is needed for the water heater?
o: A larger TPR valve installed in place of the original
A second water heater installed in series with the first
A thermal expansion control, such as an expansion tank
A pressure booster pump installed on the cold water line
en.e: Per the IRC (P2903.4), where a check valve, backflow preventer or pressure-reducing valve creates a closed system, thermal expansion control is required, because heated water has nowhere to expand.

en.q: Per the IRC, shower and tub-shower valves must limit the maximum outlet temperature to:
o: 100 degrees F
120 degrees F
140 degrees F
160 degrees F
en.e: Per the IRC (P2708.4), individual shower and tub-shower valves must be pressure-balance, thermostatic or combination types with a limit stop set at no more than 120 degrees F to prevent scalding.

en.q: Per the IRC, what is the minimum distance from the center of a toilet to a side wall or obstruction?
o: 12 inches
15 inches
18 inches
21 inches
en.e: Per the IRC (R307.1 and P2705.1), a water closet must be at least 15 inches from its center to any side wall or obstruction, and 30 inches center to center from an adjacent fixture.

en.q: Per the IRC, what is the minimum clear space in front of a toilet?
o: 15 inches
21 inches
30 inches
36 inches
en.e: Per the IRC (Figure R307.1), a clear space of at least 21 inches is required in front of a water closet, lavatory or bidet.

en.q: A toilet rocks when the inspector applies light pressure, and the floor around its base is soft. What is the most appropriate recommendation?
o: Tighten the closet bolts as hard as possible until the toilet stops moving
Have the toilet reset and the subfloor checked by a plumber
Run a bead of caulk around the base of the toilet and take no other action
No action, because all toilets move slightly when pressure is applied
en.e: A loose toilet can break its wax seal and leak, and a soft floor suggests water damage below. Resetting the toilet and checking the subfloor deal with both.

en.q: An exterior hose bibb has no vacuum breaker or other backflow protection. Why is that a concern?
o: The hose bibb will freeze sooner in the winter months
Contaminated water can be siphoned back into the supply
The water pressure at the other fixtures will drop
The hose bibb will leak continuously from its handle
en.e: A hose left in a bucket of chemicals or a puddle can siphon contaminated water back into the supply if pressure drops. Per the IRC (P2902), hose connections need backflow protection, such as a vacuum breaker.

en.q: What is the purpose of an air gap or a high loop on a dishwasher drain line?
o: To make the dishwasher drain more quickly into the sink drain
To keep sink wastewater from flowing back into the dishwasher
To cool the hot dishwasher discharge before it reaches the trap
To reduce noise from the drain pump during the drain cycle
en.e: A dishwasher drain must be protected from backflow. Per the IRC (P2717), an air gap or a drain line looped up and fastened to the underside of the counter keeps sink water from siphoning into the dishwasher.

en.q: Per the IRC, on a faucet or fixture fitting, which side is the hot water supply connected to?
o: The left side
The right side
The top
Either side, as long as it is labeled
en.e: Per the IRC (P2722.2), hot water must be connected to the left side of the fitting as the user faces it. Reversed supplies can cause scalding surprises.

en.q: In a house built in the 1950s, the sewer lateral is a black, fiber-based pipe. What is the most appropriate recommendation?
o: No action, because this type of pipe lasts for the life of the house
Recommend a sewer camera inspection by a qualified plumber
Recommend replacing all of the water supply lines inside the house
Recommend adding an air admittance valve on the main building drain
en.e: Bituminous fiber (Orangeburg) pipe was used from about the 1940s through the 1970s and tends to deform, blister and collapse. Underground sewer lines are outside a visual inspection, so a camera inspection is the appropriate referral.

en.q: Under typical standards of practice, which of these is the home inspector NOT required to do?
o: Operate plumbing fixtures to check function and drainage
Inspect the water heater and its venting
Determine whether the water supply is safe to drink
Describe the location of the main water shut-off valve
en.e: Inspectors run fixtures, check drainage, inspect the water heater and identify shut-offs, but testing water quality or potability is excluded and needs a laboratory test.

en.q: Under typical standards of practice, inspecting private wells, septic systems and water-treatment equipment is:
o: Required on every inspection, whether or not the property has them
Not required, unless agreed as an added service
Required only for properties located in rural areas
Required only if the client asks during the inspection
en.e: Wells, septic systems, water softeners and filters are excluded from typical standards of practice. They may be inspected as ancillary services by qualified inspectors where agreed.

en.q: While walking into a basement, the inspector smells a strong odor of natural gas. What is the most appropriate first action?
o: Turn on the basement lights to find the source of the leak
Leave, avoid ignition sources, and call the utility from outside
Light a match or lighter near the pipes to locate the leak
Continue the inspection and mention the odor in the report
en.e: A strong gas odor is an immediate danger. Avoid switches and flames, get everyone out, and call the utility or emergency services from outside. The condition must also be reported.

en.q: Per the IRC, what is installed on a gas supply line at the appliance inlet to catch debris and moisture before they reach the controls?
o: A pressure-relief valve
A sediment trap (drip leg)
A dielectric union
A backflow preventer
en.e: Per the IRC (G2419.4), a sediment trap must be installed downstream of the shut-off valve as close to the inlet of the appliance as practical, with exceptions for some appliances such as illuminating appliances, ranges, clothes dryers and outdoor grills.

en.q: Per the IRC, the shut-off valve for a gas appliance must be in the same room as the appliance and within how far of it?
o: 3 feet
6 feet
10 feet
25 feet
en.e: Per the IRC (G2420.5.1), each appliance must have an accessible shut-off valve in the same room and within 6 feet of the appliance (with limited exceptions, such as for some fireplaces and vented decorative appliances).

en.q: Per the IRC, which installation of a flexible gas appliance connector is NOT permitted?
o: Running the connector through a wall, floor or ceiling
Connecting a range to a gas outlet behind it
Using a listed connector no more than 6 feet long
Using a connector in the same room as the appliance
en.e: Per the IRC (G2422.1.2), appliance connectors must not pass through walls, floors, ceilings or appliance housings (with limited exceptions) and generally must not exceed 6 feet in length.

en.q: Corrugated stainless steel tubing (CSST) gas piping is found in a house. Per the IRC, what is required to reduce the risk of damage from lightning?
o: Painting the tubing with a fire-resistant coating
Bonding it to the grounding system with a 6 AWG copper jumper
Insulating the tubing with closed-cell foam sleeves
Replacing all of the tubing with rigid copper pipe
en.e: Per the IRC (G2411.1.1), CSST (other than the arc-resistant jacketed types listed for less) must be bonded to the electrical service grounding system with a bonding jumper at least 6 AWG copper. Missing bonding should be reported for evaluation.

en.q: A sump pump discharges just outside the foundation wall, and the water flows straight back toward the house. What should the inspector recommend?
o: No action, because the pump is cycling and working properly
Extending the discharge away from the foundation
Turning the pump off so that it does not run so often
Adding a second pump in the same pit beside the first one
en.e: Water discharged at the foundation can re-enter the soil around the basement and cycle back into the sump. The discharge should carry the water well away from the house.

en.q: What is a common reason old cast iron drain pipes fail?
o: They soften and melt during hot summer weather
Internal corrosion and cracking
They expand and split when hot water flows through them
They attract termites, which eat the joints between pipes
en.e: Cast iron corrodes from the inside, and horizontal runs can crack or rot along the bottom where water flows. Stains, rust scale or leaks should be reported for evaluation.

en.q: Water is dripping from the ceiling below a second-floor shower, but only while the shower is in use and the curtain is closed. What is the most likely source?
o: A leak in the supply line that runs constantly
A leaking shower pan, drain or enclosure
Condensation from the attic
A roof leak
en.e: A leak that appears only during shower use points to the shower pan, drain connection or enclosure (tile, grout or door seals). A supply leak would usually be continuous.

en.q: Supply pipes in an unheated crawl space have no insulation or heat tape in a cold-climate house. What is the risk?
o: The pipes will sweat in winter
The pipes can freeze and burst
The water will taste bad
The pipes will vibrate
en.e: Water pipes in unheated spaces in cold climates are exposed to freezing. Insulating, heat tracing or relocating them reduces the risk.

en.q: The inspector hears a loud bang in the pipes each time a faucet or washing machine valve shuts off quickly. What is this condition called?
o: Water hammer
Cross-connection
Back-siphonage
Trap siphonage
en.e: Water hammer is a pressure surge when flowing water stops suddenly. It can damage pipes and fittings. High pressure makes it worse; water hammer arrestors or a pressure-reducing valve can help.

en.q: Under typical standards of practice, what must an inspector describe about the water heater?
o: Its remaining life in years, based on the serial number
Its energy source
Its purchase price and the cost of a replacement unit
Its manufacturer's warranty terms and registration status
en.e: Standards such as InterNACHI's call for describing the water heating equipment, including the energy source, and inspecting its venting and relief valve. Predicting remaining life is not required.

en.q: A gas water heater has rust and scorch marks around the burner access opening, and the inspector sees flames spilling out of the combustion chamber when the burner fires. What is the most appropriate action?
o: Adjust the gas valve to reduce the flame size and continue the inspection
Report it as a hazard needing prompt evaluation by a gas technician
Report it as normal for gas water heaters that are more than a few years old
Recommend cleaning the scorched area with a wire brush and repainting it
en.e: Flame rollout and scorching suggest a blocked flue or combustion problem that can cause fire or carbon monoxide hazards. It needs prompt evaluation by a qualified technician.

en.q: Shortly after a gas water heater fires, the inspector holds a mirror at the draft hood and it fogs up, and the top of the tank shows heat damage. What does this indicate?
o: Normal operation for an atmospheric water heater on startup
Flue gases spilling at the draft hood (backdrafting)
The burner is too small for the size of the tank
The water temperature is set too low on the gas valve
en.e: Fogging and heat damage at the draft hood show that flue gases are spilling into the room, which can expose occupants to carbon monoxide. A qualified technician should evaluate the venting.

en.q: A basement bathroom is below the level of the sewer line. What does it usually need?
o: An S-trap on each fixture to hold back sewer gas
A sewage ejector pump in a sealed, vented basin
A larger water heater to serve the lower level
A pressure-reducing valve on the water service
en.e: Fixtures below the sewer need a sewage ejector (a pump in a sealed basin with its own vent) to lift waste up to the building drain. A sump pump is for groundwater, not sewage.

en.q: Under typical standards of practice, which of these does the inspector inspect in the plumbing system?
o: Drain, waste and vent piping that is visible
Underground sewer laterals
Interior of water supply pipes inside walls
Fire sprinkler systems
en.e: Inspectors inspect the visible water supply and drain, waste and vent systems. Underground and concealed piping and fire sprinkler systems are excluded.

en.q: A clothes washer standpipe is installed inside a laundry room wall. Per the IRC, the standpipe should extend at least ___ and no more than ___ above its trap weir.
o: 6 inches; 18 inches
18 inches; 42 inches
30 inches; 60 inches
42 inches; 72 inches
en.e: Per the IRC (P2706.1.2), a standpipe must extend at least 18 inches and no more than 42 inches above the trap weir. A short standpipe can overflow; a tall one can siphon the trap.

en.q: Per the IRC, overhead service-drop conductors (up to 150 volts to ground) must be at least how high above a residential driveway?
o: 8 feet
10 feet
12 feet
18 feet
en.e: Per the IRC (E3604.2.1), service drops must clear residential property and driveways by 12 feet, finished grade and sidewalks by 10 feet, and public streets, alleys and roads by 18 feet.

en.q: Per the IRC, overhead service-drop conductors must be at least how high above a public street?
o: 10 feet
12 feet
15 feet
18 feet
en.e: Per the IRC (E3604.2.1), service conductors over public streets, alleys, roads and parking areas subject to truck traffic need at least 18 feet of clearance.

en.q: Per the IRC, open overhead service conductors must be kept at least how far from windows that open, doors, porches and decks?
o: 1 foot
3 feet
6 feet
10 feet
en.e: Per the IRC (E3604.1), open service conductors must have a clearance of at least 3 feet from windows that open, doors, porches, balconies, ladders, stairs, fire escapes and similar locations.

en.q: What is the purpose of the drip loop in the service-drop conductors at the service head?
o: To make water run off the low point of the loop instead of into the service head
To give the utility extra wire for future upgrades
To reduce the voltage
To ground the service
en.e: The conductors dip below the service head so that rain runs down to the low point and drips off, rather than following the wires into the conduit and panel.

en.q: The inspector notices rust and water stains inside the main panel, and the service head on the mast above is missing its cap. What is the most likely cause?
o: Condensation from the air conditioner
Water entering through the damaged service head and running down the service conduit
A plumbing leak in the attic
Normal for older panels
en.e: A damaged or missing weatherhead lets rain into the service raceway, which carries water into the panel. Water in a panel is a shock and fire hazard that needs an electrician.

en.q: Per the IRC, what is the minimum depth of working space in front of a residential electrical panel?
o: 24 inches
30 inches
36 inches
48 inches
en.e: Per the IRC (E3405.2), the working space in front of panels must be at least 36 inches deep, at least 30 inches wide (or the width of the equipment) and at least 6-1/2 feet high.

en.q: Per the IRC, what is the minimum width of the working space in front of an electrical panel?
o: 24 inches
30 inches, or the width of the equipment if greater
36 inches
48 inches
en.e: Per the IRC (E3405.2), the work space must be at least 30 inches wide or the width of the equipment, whichever is greater, with doors able to open at least 90 degrees.

en.q: Per the IRC, an electrical panel containing overcurrent devices must NOT be located in which of these places?
o: A garage
A basement
A utility room
A clothes closet or bathroom
en.e: Per the IRC (E3705.7), overcurrent devices must not be located in clothes closets, in bathrooms or over the steps of a stairway.

en.q: In a panel, the inspector finds two wires connected under a single breaker terminal screw. The breaker is not marked for two conductors. What is this condition, and what is the concern?
o: A split bus; normal
A double tap; the terminal may not clamp both wires securely, which can cause overheating
A bootleg ground; reverse polarity
A multiwire branch circuit; required by code
en.e: Most breaker terminals are listed for one conductor. Two wires under one screw (a double tap) can loosen and overheat. A few breakers are listed for two conductors, so the inspector checks the labeling and recommends correction by an electrician if not listed.

en.q: In a main panel, two white neutral wires are found under one terminal screw on the neutral bar. Why is this a concern?
o: It is required in main panels
Each neutral should have its own terminal so that one circuit can be serviced without disturbing the other and connections stay tight
It causes reverse polarity
It makes the breakers trip too often
en.e: The NEC (408.41) requires each grounded (neutral) conductor to end in its own terminal. Shared terminals can loosen, and disconnecting one neutral could interrupt another circuit's neutral.

en.q: In a subpanel (not the service equipment), the neutral bar is bonded to the metal enclosure, and the grounds and neutrals are mixed on the same bar. What should be reported?
o: Nothing, because that is how all panels are wired
The neutrals and equipment grounds should be separated, with the neutral bar isolated from the enclosure
The subpanel needs a larger main breaker
The subpanel should be moved outdoors
en.e: Neutrals and grounds are bonded together only at the service equipment. In a subpanel, a bonded neutral puts normal current on the grounding path and metal parts, so they must be separated (a four-wire feeder).

en.q: Where is the main bonding jumper that connects the neutral to the equipment grounding system supposed to be?
o: At the service equipment only
In every subpanel
At every receptacle
At the meter only
en.e: The neutral and grounding systems are bonded only at the service (the main disconnect). Bonding elsewhere creates parallel paths for neutral current.

en.q: Per the IRC, a single ground rod electrode must be at least how long?
o: 4 feet
6 feet
8 feet
10 feet
en.e: Per the IRC (E3608.1.4), rod electrodes must be at least 8 feet long and driven so that at least 8 feet is in contact with soil. Rods of 5/8 inch diameter, or 1/2 inch if listed, are typical.

en.q: Per the IRC, when two ground rods are used, how far apart must they be?
o: 2 feet
6 feet
10 feet
25 feet
en.e: Per the IRC (E3608.4 and E3608.1.4), a single rod with resistance over 25 ohms needs a supplemental electrode. Where more than one rod is used, they must be at least 6 feet apart.

en.q: Why must a metal underground water pipe used as a grounding electrode be supplemented by an additional electrode?
o: Water pipes conduct electricity too well
The pipe may later be replaced with plastic or isolated, so the grounding would be lost
Water pipes cannot be bonded
Supplementing is optional
en.e: Per the IRC (E3608.1.1), a metal underground water pipe electrode must be supplemented by another electrode, because future plastic repairs could break the path to earth.

en.q: A 20-amp breaker protects a circuit wired with 14 AWG copper. What is the concern?
o: None, because 14 AWG is rated for 20 amps
The wire is too small for the breaker, so it can overheat before the breaker trips
The breaker is too small for the wire
The circuit will have reverse polarity
en.e: 14 AWG copper is limited to 15 amps of overcurrent protection. A 20-amp breaker on 14 AWG wire (overfusing) is a fire hazard and should be corrected by an electrician.

en.q: Under the general rule, what is the maximum overcurrent protection for 12 AWG copper branch-circuit wire?
o: 15 amps
20 amps
30 amps
40 amps
en.e: Under the small-conductor rule in the NEC (240.4(D)) and the IRC, copper wire is limited to 15 amps for 14 AWG, 20 amps for 12 AWG and 30 amps for 10 AWG.

en.q: A 30-amp double-pole breaker serves an electric water heater. What is the smallest copper wire normally allowed on it?
o: 14 AWG
12 AWG
10 AWG
6 AWG
en.e: Under the general rule, 10 AWG copper may be protected at up to 30 amps. Smaller wire on a 30-amp breaker would be overfused.

en.q: Solid-conductor aluminum branch-circuit wiring was commonly installed in homes from about the mid-1960s to the mid-1970s. What is the main concern?
o: It cannot carry 120 volts
Connections can loosen and overheat, creating a fire risk, especially at devices not rated for aluminum
It always has reverse polarity
It attracts lightning
en.e: Single-strand aluminum branch wiring expands, oxidizes and creeps at terminals, which can lead to overheating. The inspector should report it and recommend evaluation by an electrician familiar with approved repair methods.

en.q: Which of these is a widely recognized repair method for solid-conductor aluminum branch wiring?
o: Wrapping each connection in electrical tape
Replacing breakers with larger ones
Pigtailing to copper with special connectors listed for the purpose, such as the COPALUM crimp or AlumiConn
Painting the wires with anti-rust paint
en.e: The CPSC recognizes copper pigtailing using the COPALUM crimp or AlumiConn connectors as repair methods. Ordinary twist-on connectors are not a recommended repair.

en.q: The service-entrance conductors are multi-strand aluminum. How should this generally be reported?
o: As a common, acceptable installation when properly installed and terminated
As a fire hazard that must be replaced with copper
As the same hazard as solid aluminum branch wiring
As a sign of an illegal service
en.e: Stranded aluminum service and feeder conductors are common and acceptable. The known problems apply to small-gauge solid aluminum branch wiring. Terminations should be tight, often with antioxidant compound.

en.q: An inspector identifies a Federal Pacific Electric (FPE) panel with Stab-Lok breakers. What is the most appropriate report comment?
o: No comment, because brand names are not reported
Note that these breakers have a history of failing to trip under overload, and recommend evaluation by a licensed electrician
State that the panel will catch fire within a year
Recommend replacing the breakers with larger ones
en.e: FPE Stab-Lok breakers have a widely reported history of failing to trip. The inspector should report the panel type and the concern and refer it to an electrician, without predicting exact outcomes.

en.q: Zinsco (and some Sylvania-Zinsco) panels are reported as a concern mainly because:
o: They have too many breaker spaces
Breakers can overheat and melt or fuse to the bus bar, so they may not trip
They are only rated for 30 amps
They are always installed outdoors
en.e: Zinsco breakers are known for loose connections that overheat and can weld to the aluminum bus, defeating protection. The panel should be evaluated by an electrician.

en.q: In a fuse panel, a 30-amp fuse is installed on a circuit wired with 14 AWG copper. What is the concern, and what device helps prevent it?
o: No concern; a bigger fuse is safer
Overfusing; Type S fuse adapters limit the size of fuse that can be installed
Reverse polarity; a GFCI fixes it
Undervoltage; a larger wire fixes it
en.e: A 30-amp fuse on 14 AWG wire lets the wire overheat. Type S (non-tamperable) fuses and adapters keep a larger fuse from being screwed into a smaller circuit.

en.q: Knob-and-tube wiring is found buried under loose-fill insulation in an attic. What is the concern?
o: None, because insulation protects the wires
The wiring was designed to release heat into open air, and burying it can cause overheating; it also has no equipment ground
The wiring will cause the insulation to get wet
The wiring is always aluminum
en.e: Knob-and-tube depends on open air for cooling, and the NEC (394.12) prohibits its use in hollow spaces with insulation that envelops the conductors. Its age, brittle insulation and lack of a ground also call for evaluation by an electrician.

en.q: A plug-in receptacle tester shows "open ground" at a three-prong receptacle. What does this mean?
o: The hot and neutral are reversed
The receptacle's equipment ground is not connected
The circuit has no power
The receptacle is GFCI-protected
en.e: An open ground means the grounding terminal has no path to ground, so the third prong gives a false sense of protection. It should be corrected or, where allowed, protected with a GFCI and labeled.

en.q: A receptacle tester shows "hot/neutral reversed" at a receptacle. What is the hazard?
o: The fixture's shell or a device's switch may be energized even when the device is switched off
The circuit breaker will be too large
The receptacle will not work
The wiring will turn to aluminum
en.e: Reverse polarity puts the hot conductor on the neutral side, so lamp shells and some appliance parts can remain energized when switched off. It should be corrected by an electrician.

en.q: Why can a "bootleg ground" fool a standard three-light receptacle tester?
o: It makes the tester's lights flicker
The neutral is jumpered to the ground screw, so the tester sees a correct wiring pattern even though there is no true ground
It removes power from the circuit
It reverses the hot and neutral
en.e: A bootleg ground connects the grounding terminal to the neutral at the receptacle. A basic tester reads it as correct, but the metal parts can become energized if the neutral fails. Grounding receptacles on older ungrounded wiring should raise suspicion.

en.q: An older house has two-prong receptacles on ungrounded wiring. Under the NEC, which is an acceptable way to replace a two-prong receptacle with a three-prong one?
o: Install a three-prong receptacle with nothing connected to the ground screw, without any label
Protect the receptacle with a GFCI and label it "No Equipment Ground"
Connect the ground screw to the neutral screw
Connect the ground screw to a water pipe in the wall
en.e: The NEC (406.4(D)) allows a three-prong receptacle on an ungrounded circuit if it is GFCI-protected and marked "No Equipment Ground" (or the grounding conductor is properly added).

en.q: What is the main purpose of a GFCI (ground-fault circuit interrupter)?
o: To prevent wiring fires caused by arcing
To protect people from electric shock by cutting power when current leaks to ground
To prevent overloads on the circuit
To raise the voltage on long circuits
en.e: A GFCI compares current on the hot and neutral and trips when about 4 to 6 milliamps leaks to ground, protecting people from shock. AFCIs address arcing; breakers protect wiring from overloads.

en.q: What is the main purpose of an AFCI (arc-fault circuit interrupter)?
o: To reduce the risk of fire by detecting dangerous arcing in the wiring
To protect people from shock in wet locations
To prevent power surges from lightning
To reduce the electric bill
en.e: AFCIs detect the electrical signature of arcing faults, such as damaged cords or loose connections, and open the circuit to prevent fires. They are not a substitute for GFCIs in wet locations.

en.q: Per the IRC, which location does NOT generally require GFCI protection for 125-volt, 15- and 20-amp receptacles?
o: A bathroom
A garage
An outdoor receptacle
A bedroom
en.e: Per the IRC (E3902), GFCI protection is required in bathrooms, garages, outdoors, crawl spaces, unfinished basements, kitchen countertop areas, within 6 feet of sinks and in laundry areas. Bedrooms require AFCI protection, not GFCI.

en.q: Per the IRC, which kitchen receptacles require GFCI protection?
o: Only the receptacle closest to the sink
All receptacles serving the countertop surfaces
Only receptacles behind the refrigerator
None, if the kitchen has a window
en.e: Per the IRC (E3902), all 125-volt, 15- and 20-amp receptacles that serve kitchen countertop surfaces require GFCI protection.

en.q: Per the IRC, which of these locations requires AFCI protection for 120-volt, 15- and 20-amp branch circuits?
o: An outdoor receptacle
A crawl space
A hallway
A bathroom
en.e: Per the IRC (E3902), AFCI protection is required for circuits supplying outlets in kitchens, family rooms, dining rooms, living rooms, parlors, libraries, dens, bedrooms, sunrooms, recreation rooms, closets, hallways, laundry areas and similar rooms.

en.q: Per the IRC, along a general-use wall, receptacles must be placed so that no point along the floor line is more than how far from a receptacle?
o: 4 feet
6 feet
10 feet
12 feet
en.e: Per the IRC (E3901.2.1), no point along the floor line of a wall may be more than 6 feet from a receptacle, which means receptacles are typically no more than 12 feet apart.

en.q: Per the IRC, kitchen countertop receptacles must be installed so that no point along the wall line of the countertop is more than how far from a receptacle?
o: 12 inches
24 inches
36 inches
48 inches
en.e: Per the IRC (E3901.4.1), countertop receptacles must be placed so that no point along the wall line is more than 24 inches from a receptacle. Every countertop space 12 inches or wider needs a receptacle.

en.q: Per the IRC, at least one receptacle must be installed within how far of the outside edge of each bathroom basin?
o: 12 inches
24 inches
36 inches
6 feet
en.e: Per the IRC (E3901.6), at least one wall receptacle must be within 36 inches of the outside edge of each basin.

en.q: Per the IRC, how many 20-amp small-appliance branch circuits must serve the kitchen countertop receptacles at minimum?
o: One
Two
Three
Four
en.e: Per the IRC (E3703.2), at least two 20-amp small-appliance branch circuits are required for the receptacles in the kitchen, pantry, breakfast and dining areas.

en.q: Per the IRC, what type of receptacles are generally required in new dwelling installations to reduce the risk of children inserting objects?
o: Tamper-resistant receptacles
Isolated-ground receptacles
Hospital-grade receptacles
Switched receptacles
en.e: Per the IRC (E4002.14), 125-volt, 15- and 20-amp receptacles in dwellings generally must be listed tamper-resistant, with a few exceptions, such as receptacles more than 5-1/2 feet above the floor.

en.q: In an attic, the inspector finds several wire splices wrapped in tape and lying on top of the insulation, not inside any box. What should the inspector report?
o: It is acceptable if the tape is new
It is a fire and shock hazard; splices must be in accessible, covered junction boxes, and an electrician should correct them
It is a cosmetic issue
Only the insulation needs replacing
en.e: Splices must be in approved boxes with covers so that heat and sparks are contained and the connections are protected. Open splices are a common safety defect.

en.q: While inspecting a panel, the inspector finds an open knockout where a breaker or cover piece is missing. What is the concern?
o: None, because it helps cool the panel
It exposes energized parts to fingers and objects, and the opening should be closed with an approved filler
It allows too much light into the panel
It means the panel is overloaded
en.e: Unused openings in panels must be closed with approved fillers so that no one can contact live parts. InterNACHI's standards specifically call for reporting this.

en.q: The dead-front cover of a panel is held on with long, pointed sheet-metal screws. Why is this a concern?
o: They are hard to remove
Pointed screws can pierce the insulation of wires inside the panel and energize the cover
They rust faster
They make the panel look unprofessional only
en.e: Panel covers should be fastened with the blunt-tipped screws made for the panel. Sharp screws can damage conductors behind the cover.

en.q: What does a melted or discolored wire insulation and scorch marks on a breaker indicate?
o: Overheating, such as from a loose connection or overload
Normal aging
A properly sized breaker
Too much insulation in the attic
en.e: Discoloration and melting show the connection or conductor has overheated. That is a fire hazard needing prompt evaluation by an electrician.

en.q: Before removing the dead-front cover of an electrical panel, what is a sensible first step?
o: Turn off the main breaker to protect yourself
Pry the cover off from the bottom
Check the cover and surroundings for hazards, such as water, rust, scorching or energized metal (for example with a non-contact voltage tester), and stand safely
Ask the homeowner to remove it
en.e: Inspectors normally do not turn off the main breaker during an inspection. They check for hazards first and wear appropriate protection. If conditions look unsafe, they do not remove the cover and report why.

en.q: The main panel is in a damp basement corner, the cover is rusted, and the inspector would have to stand in water to reach it. What is the most appropriate action?
o: Remove the cover carefully anyway
Do not open the panel; report the condition, that the interior was not inspected and why, and recommend evaluation by an electrician
Turn off the main breaker and open it
Skip the panel and leave it out of the report
en.e: Standards of practice do not require inspectors to enter or work in unsafe conditions. They must report what was not inspected and the reason.

en.q: A homeowner has connected a portable generator to the house by plugging it into a dryer receptacle with a male-to-male cord. What is the hazard?
o: The generator will run out of fuel faster
Power can backfeed onto utility lines, endangering line workers, and the cord's exposed prongs can be energized
The dryer will run on gas
The breakers will become larger
en.e: Without a transfer switch or approved interlock, a generator can backfeed the utility system and energize lines being repaired. A male-to-male cord also has live exposed prongs. This is a serious safety hazard.

en.q: Per the NEC, what color identifies a grounded (neutral) conductor in branch-circuit wiring?
o: Green
White or gray
Red
Black
en.e: Grounded (neutral) conductors are white or gray. Equipment grounding conductors are green, green with yellow stripes or bare. A white wire used as a hot conductor (such as in a switch loop) should be re-identified, for example with tape.

en.q: Per the IRC, where a stairway has six or more risers, a wall switch controlling the stair lighting must be located:
o: Only at the top
Only at the bottom
At each floor level
Anywhere within 25 feet
en.e: Per the IRC (E3903.3), where a stairway between floor levels has six or more risers, a wall switch must be provided at each floor level so that the lighting can be controlled from both ends.

en.q: Under typical standards of practice, how many receptacles must the inspector test?
o: Every receptacle in the house
A representative number
Only the ones the client points out
Only receptacles in the kitchen
en.e: Standards such as ASHI and InterNACHI require inspecting a representative number of switches, lighting fixtures and receptacles, plus all GFCI devices that are found and accessible.

en.q: Under typical standards of practice, which of these is the inspector NOT required to do when inspecting the electrical system?
o: Describe the main disconnect's amperage rating if it is labeled
Report the presence of solid-conductor aluminum branch wiring if readily visible
Measure the amperage or voltage of the service
Test GFCI devices that are accessible
en.e: Inspectors describe and inspect the service and distribution and test GFCIs, but they are not required to measure voltage or amperage or perform load calculations.

en.q: A central air conditioner has run for 15 minutes. The air at the supply register is only 5 degrees F cooler than the return air. How should this be reported?
o: As normal, because any temperature drop is acceptable
As below the commonly expected range of roughly 15 to 20 degrees F, with evaluation recommended by an HVAC technician
As a sign that the system is oversized
As an electrical defect
en.e: A temperature split well below the typical range suggests low refrigerant, airflow problems or a failing compressor. The split is a screening tool, so the inspector refers the system rather than diagnosing it.

en.q: The outdoor temperature is 50 degrees F on inspection day. What should the inspector generally do about testing the central air conditioner?
o: Run it for at least an hour to be sure it works
Not operate it, because running it in low outdoor temperatures can damage the compressor, and report that it was not tested
Run it with the outdoor unit covered
Bypass the low-temperature lockout
en.e: Manufacturers typically warn against operating cooling below about 60 to 65 degrees F. Standards of practice do not require operating equipment when conditions could damage it; the limitation is reported.

en.q: In winter, the outdoor unit of a heat pump stops its fan and releases a cloud of steam for a few minutes. What is most likely happening?
o: The compressor is on fire
The unit is in a normal defrost cycle, melting frost off the outdoor coil
The refrigerant is leaking
The unit is overheating
en.e: Heat pumps periodically reverse to warm the outdoor coil and melt frost. Steam and a stopped fan during this cycle are normal; a coil that stays encased in ice is not.

en.q: On a heat pump thermostat, what does "emergency heat" or "auxiliary heat" usually refer to?
o: Backup heating, often electric resistance strips, used when the heat pump cannot keep up or has failed
A second outdoor unit
A gas fireplace connected to the thermostat
Turning the system off in an emergency
en.e: Heat pumps use supplemental heat (usually electric strips) in very cold weather, during defrost, or when "emergency heat" is selected because the compressor has failed.

en.q: When a gas furnace's blower starts, the burner flames waver and lean noticeably. What may this indicate?
o: Normal operation
A possible breach in the heat exchanger letting blower air disturb the flames
A dirty air filter only
An oversized gas line
en.e: Flame movement when the blower starts can indicate a cracked heat exchanger. The inspector should report it and recommend evaluation by a qualified HVAC technician, because of the carbon monoxide risk.

en.q: Under typical standards of practice, is the home inspector required to inspect the interior of a furnace's heat exchanger?
o: Yes, always
No; it is not readily accessible and requires dismantling, which is beyond a home inspection
Only on furnaces less than 10 years old
Only if the client asks
en.e: Standards such as ASHI and InterNACHI exclude inspecting heat exchanger interiors. Inspectors report visible signs that suggest a problem and refer to an HVAC technician.

en.q: Scorch marks and melted wire insulation are found just outside the burner compartment of a gas furnace. What condition do these most likely indicate?
o: Flame rollout, often from a blocked flue or heat exchanger problem
Normal wear
An oversized air filter
A failed thermostat
en.e: Flames rolling out of the combustion chamber leave scorching around the burner area. Rollout is a fire and carbon monoxide hazard that needs prompt evaluation by a qualified technician.

en.q: Per the IRC (fuel gas provisions), the standard method for indoor combustion air requires at least how many cubic feet of room volume per 1,000 Btu/h of appliance input?
o: 10 cubic feet
25 cubic feet
50 cubic feet
100 cubic feet
en.e: Per the IRC (G2407.5.1), the standard method requires at least 50 cubic feet of space per 1,000 Btu/h of total input rating of all appliances in the space.

en.q: A basement mechanical room holds a 100,000 Btu/h furnace and a 40,000 Btu/h water heater. Using the IRC standard method for indoor combustion air, what minimum room volume is required?
o: 2,000 cubic feet
5,000 cubic feet
7,000 cubic feet
14,000 cubic feet
en.e: The total input is 140,000 Btu/h, which is 140 times 50 cubic feet, or 7,000 cubic feet. A smaller space needs openings to adjoining rooms or the outdoors.

en.q: Per the IRC, when combustion air comes from outdoors through two vertical ducts, each opening must have a free area of at least:
o: 1 square inch per 1,000 Btu/h
1 square inch per 2,000 Btu/h
1 square inch per 3,000 Btu/h
1 square inch per 4,000 Btu/h
en.e: Per the IRC (G2407.6.1), two openings that connect directly or through vertical ducts to the outdoors need 1 square inch per 4,000 Btu/h each; horizontal ducts need 1 square inch per 2,000 Btu/h each.

en.q: Per the IRC, when two permanent openings connect an appliance room to other indoor space for combustion air, where must they be located?
o: Both near the floor
Both near the ceiling
One within 12 inches of the top and one within 12 inches of the bottom of the enclosure
Anywhere, as long as they are the same size
en.e: Per the IRC (G2407.5.3), one opening must start within 12 inches of the top and one within 12 inches of the bottom. Each needs 1 square inch per 1,000 Btu/h, and no less than 100 square inches.

en.q: Per the IRC, which fuel-burning appliance may generally be installed in a bedroom or bathroom?
o: A standard atmospheric gas water heater
An unvented gas room heater
A direct-vent appliance that takes all combustion air from outdoors
A gas furnace that takes combustion air from the room
en.e: Per the IRC (G2406.2), fuel-fired appliances are generally prohibited in bedrooms, bathrooms and their closets unless they are direct-vent, or one of the other limited exceptions applies, such as a closet with solid self-closing door and outdoor combustion air.

en.q: How should the horizontal section of a gas appliance vent connector be sloped?
o: Downward toward the chimney
Level
Upward toward the chimney or vent, at least 1/4 inch per foot
It does not matter
en.e: Per the IRC (G2427.10.4), vent connectors must rise at least 1/4 inch per foot toward the vent or chimney so that hot gases flow up and out.

en.q: What is the commonly required clearance between a single-wall metal vent connector serving a gas appliance and combustible materials?
o: 1 inch
3 inches
6 inches
18 inches
en.e: A single-wall metal connector for listed gas appliances with draft hoods generally needs 6 inches of clearance to combustibles, while Type B double-wall vent typically needs 1 inch (always follow the listing).

en.q: In the attic, the inspector finds single-wall metal vent pipe from a gas furnace passing through the attic to the roof. What should be reported?
o: Acceptable, because metal does not burn
Single-wall metal vent pipe is not permitted to pass through attics or concealed spaces; recommend correction by a qualified HVAC contractor
The pipe needs to be painted
The pipe needs more insulation wrapped around it
en.e: Per the IRC (G2427.10.2), single-wall metal pipe must not pass through any attic, inside wall, concealed space or floor. Type B vent or another listed system must be used.

en.q: What type of venting is typically used for a high-efficiency (90 percent or higher AFUE) condensing gas furnace?
o: An unlined masonry chimney
Single-wall galvanized pipe
Plastic pipe, such as PVC or CPVC, as specified by the manufacturer
Type B vent shared with a water heater
en.e: Condensing (Category IV) furnaces produce cool, wet, positive-pressure exhaust. They usually vent through plastic pipe specified by the manufacturer and need a condensate drain.

en.q: An older furnace was replaced with a 95 percent sidewall-vented model, leaving an atmospheric gas water heater as the only appliance venting into a large masonry chimney. What concern should the inspector report?
o: None, because removing the furnace helps the water heater
The chimney may now be oversized for the water heater, causing poor draft and condensation; recommend evaluation by a qualified technician
The water heater must also be removed
The chimney will become too hot
en.e: An "orphaned" water heater in a chimney sized for two appliances may not draft well, and flue gases can condense and damage the chimney. A liner or other correction is often needed.

en.q: How can a home inspector check an atmospheric gas water heater or furnace for spillage at the draft hood?
o: After a few minutes of operation, hold a mirror or smoke source near the draft hood and look for fogging or smoke being pushed out
Place a hand inside the flue while the burner is on
Measure the gas pressure at the valve
Shut off the venting and watch the flames
en.e: A mirror that fogs or smoke that is pushed away from the hood shows flue gases spilling into the room, which is a carbon monoxide risk.

en.q: An air handler in the attic has water in its auxiliary drain pan. What is the most likely cause?
o: The thermostat is set too low
The primary condensate drain is clogged or not draining properly
The refrigerant is overcharged
The attic has too much ventilation
en.e: The auxiliary pan catches water when the primary condensate drain fails. Water in the pan should be reported, and the primary drain and pan evaluated by an HVAC technician.

en.q: Per the IRC, where a cooling coil or appliance is in an attic or above a finished ceiling, what condensate protection is required?
o: None
A secondary drain, an auxiliary pan with drain, or a water-level device that shuts off the equipment if the primary drain backs up
A second air conditioner
A drain into the attic insulation
en.e: Per the IRC (M1411.3.1), where damage could result from overflow, one of these methods is required. A secondary drain should discharge where occupants will notice it, such as over a window.

en.q: Per the IRC, condensate drain piping must be at least what internal diameter and slope?
o: 1/2 inch; level
3/4 inch; at least 1/8 inch per foot
1 inch; at least 1/2 inch per foot
2 inches; at least 1/4 inch per foot
en.e: Per the IRC (M1411.3.2 and M1411.4), condensate drains must be at least 3/4 inch internal diameter and slope at least 1/8 inch per foot.

en.q: The larger refrigerant line running to an air conditioner's outdoor unit has no insulation, and it drips water in the crawl space. What is the concern?
o: None, because the lines do not need insulation
The suction line should be insulated to prevent condensation and energy loss
The smaller liquid line should be insulated instead
The line is carrying too much electricity
en.e: The larger suction line carries cold refrigerant gas back to the compressor. Without insulation it sweats, causing water damage and lost efficiency.

en.q: The suction line and the indoor coil of an air conditioner are covered with frost and ice. What is a common cause?
o: An oversized outdoor unit
Low airflow, such as from a dirty filter, or a low refrigerant charge
A thermostat that is set too high
Too much insulation on the line
en.e: Ice forms when the coil gets too cold, often from restricted airflow or low refrigerant. The inspector should report it and recommend an HVAC technician. Running the system iced can damage the compressor.

en.q: Per the NEC, the disconnect for an outdoor air conditioner unit must generally be located:
o: Inside the house next to the thermostat
Within sight of the unit and readily accessible
At least 25 feet from the unit
On the roof
en.e: The NEC (440.14) requires a disconnecting means within sight of and readily accessible from the air conditioning equipment so that a technician can safely shut it off.

en.q: Per the IRC, return air for a forced-air system must NOT be taken from which space?
o: A hallway
A living room
A bathroom, kitchen or garage
A bedroom (with proper return path)
en.e: Per the IRC (M1602.2), return air must not be taken from bathrooms, toilet rooms, kitchens, garages, mechanical rooms with fuel-burning appliances and similar spaces, to avoid spreading odors, moisture and combustion gases.

en.q: An inspector finds a return-air grille cut into the ductwork inside an attached garage. What is the concern?
o: The system can draw car exhaust, fuel vapors and other contaminants from the garage into the house
It will make the garage warmer
The grille is too small
None, because garages need return air
en.e: Openings in ducts in a garage can pull carbon monoxide and fumes into the living space and breach the fire separation. The IRC prohibits return air from garages.

en.q: Per the IRC, the passageway to a furnace in an attic must be no longer than how far from the access opening?
o: 6 feet
10 feet
20 feet
50 feet
en.e: Per the IRC (M1305.1.3), the passageway must be no more than 20 feet long measured along the center line, at least 30 inches high and 22 inches wide, with continuous solid flooring at least 24 inches wide.

en.q: Per the IRC, which of these must be provided near an appliance installed in an attic?
o: A floor drain
A smoke alarm inside the appliance
A light controlled by a switch at the passageway entrance, and a receptacle near the appliance
A window
en.e: Per the IRC (M1305.1.3.1 and E3901.12), attic appliances need a light fixture controlled by a switch at the entrance and a receptacle within 25 feet of the appliance for servicing.

en.q: A hot-water boiler's relief valve is dripping, and the pressure gauge reads about 30 psi with the system hot. The boiler normally operates at about 12 to 15 psi. What is a likely cause?
o: The thermostat is set too low
The system is over-pressurized, often from a waterlogged expansion tank or a faulty fill valve
The burner is too small
The circulator pump is running too quickly
en.e: Residential boilers usually have a 30 psi relief valve. Pressure rising to that point suggests a failed expansion tank or fill valve. A boiler technician should evaluate it.

en.q: On a steam boiler, what does the sight glass show?
o: The water level in the boiler
The flame color
The steam pressure in psi
The temperature of the supply pipes
en.e: The sight glass (gauge glass) shows the boiler water level. Steam boilers also need a low-water cutoff, because firing a dry boiler is dangerous.

en.q: Old furnace ducts are wrapped in white, fibrous tape at the joints in a 1950s home. What is the best way to report this?
o: State that it is asbestos and must be removed immediately
Scrape a sample for testing during the inspection
Note that the material may contain asbestos, advise against disturbing it, and recommend testing by a qualified professional if it will be disturbed
Do not mention it
en.e: Asbestos cannot be confirmed visually, and sampling is outside the inspection. Describing it as possibly containing asbestos and recommending professional testing is accurate and appropriate.

en.q: Per the IRC, in climates that need heating, dwellings must have heat that can maintain at least what temperature in habitable rooms?
o: 60 degrees F
65 degrees F
68 degrees F
72 degrees F
en.e: Per the IRC (R303.10), where the winter design temperature is below 60 degrees F, heating must be able to maintain at least 68 degrees F at 3 feet above the floor and 2 feet from exterior walls in all habitable rooms.

en.q: In a crawl space, a heating supply duct has come apart at a joint and is blowing warm air into the crawl space. What should the inspector recommend?
o: No action, because the warm air helps keep pipes from freezing
Repair by a qualified HVAC contractor, since the disconnected duct wastes energy and reduces heat to the rooms
Replacing the furnace
Closing all the registers
en.e: A disconnected duct dumps conditioned air into the wrong space and can draw in crawl space air. It should be reconnected and sealed.

en.q: What does AFUE mean on a furnace rating?
o: Average fan usage efficiency
Annual fuel utilization efficiency, the percentage of fuel energy delivered as useful heat over a typical season
Air filter use estimate
Automatic fuel unit emergency
en.e: AFUE is a seasonal efficiency rating. An 80 percent furnace delivers about 80 percent of the fuel's energy as heat; condensing furnaces are 90 percent or more.

en.q: Under typical standards of practice, which of these is the inspector NOT required to do when inspecting the heating system?
o: Operate the system using normal operating controls
Open readily openable access panels
Light a pilot light that is out
Describe the energy source and heating method
en.e: Standards of practice require operating the system with normal controls and describing it, but exclude lighting pilots, operating systems that are shut down and dismantling equipment.

en.q: A furnace's data plate lists an allowable temperature rise of 35 to 65 degrees F, and the inspector measures a rise of 85 degrees F between return and supply. What does this suggest?
o: A problem, such as restricted airflow, that should be evaluated by an HVAC technician
Normal, high-efficiency operation
An oversized duct system
A broken thermostat display
en.e: A rise above the listed range usually means too little air is moving over the heat exchanger, such as from a dirty filter or restricted ducts. This overheats the heat exchanger and should be evaluated.

en.q: A furnace short-cycles: it runs for a minute or two, shuts off and quickly restarts. Which is a possible cause?
o: A correctly sized system
An oversized system or a control problem, such as a faulty limit switch
A clean filter
Proper airflow
en.e: Short cycling wastes energy, increases wear and reduces comfort. The inspector reports the observation and refers it to an HVAC technician for diagnosis.

en.q: In a dry climate, what is the main way an evaporative cooler cools the air?
o: By compressing refrigerant
By evaporating water into incoming air
By burning fuel
By drawing air from the ground
en.e: Evaporative ("swamp") coolers pass air over wet pads; evaporation lowers the air temperature. They work best in hot, dry climates and need regular water and pad maintenance.

en.q: A gas furnace sits in a closet. Per the IRC, why might the closet door need louvers or openings?
o: To let light into the closet
To supply combustion air if the furnace draws air from the surrounding space
To make the furnace quieter
So that the furnace can be seen from outside the closet
en.e: Appliances that draw combustion air from the room need adequate air through openings or louvers unless they are direct-vent or have outdoor air supplied another way.

en.q: A gas furnace in an attached garage has its burners about 6 inches above the floor, and the furnace is not listed as flammable-vapor-ignition-resistant. Per the IRC, what should be reported?
o: Nothing, because furnaces are allowed anywhere
The ignition source should be at least 18 inches above the garage floor
The furnace must be at least 36 inches above the floor
The furnace should be moved into a bedroom
en.e: Per the IRC (M1307.3 and G2408.2), appliances with ignition sources in garages must have the ignition source at least 18 inches above the floor, unless listed as FVIR, because gasoline vapors collect near the floor.

en.q: Rust flakes are falling onto the burners of an older gas furnace, and the burners are covered in rust. What may this indicate?
o: Normal for every furnace
Moisture from condensation or a leak, such as from an air conditioning coil, deteriorating the furnace; recommend evaluation
An oversized filter
A new thermostat
en.e: Rust inside the burner compartment often comes from condensation, venting problems or a leaking coil above the furnace. It can lead to heat exchanger failure and should be evaluated.

en.q: How is a ductless mini-split system different from a central system?
o: It has one or more indoor air handlers connected to an outdoor unit by refrigerant lines, without supply ducts
It uses only electric resistance heat
It cannot provide heating
It requires a chimney
en.e: Mini-splits deliver conditioned air directly from wall, ceiling or floor units. Many are heat pumps that both heat and cool.

en.q: The outdoor air conditioner unit is tilted and partly blocked by dense shrubs. What should the inspector report?
o: No concern
The unit should be level, and vegetation should be cleared to provide the manufacturer's recommended airflow clearance
The unit should be enclosed in a box
The unit should be moved into the attic
en.e: Restricted airflow reduces efficiency and can damage the compressor, and a tilted unit can affect oil return and drainage. Clearances follow manufacturer instructions.

en.q: What is the main safety function of a furnace's high-limit control?
o: To start the blower on a timer
To shut off the burner if the heat exchanger area overheats
To reduce the thermostat setting at night
To adjust gas pressure
en.e: The high-limit switch shuts off the burner if temperatures get too high, such as from poor airflow. Frequent limit tripping suggests a problem to evaluate.

en.q: An unlined masonry chimney serves a gas furnace, and the inspector sees crumbled mortar and debris at the base of the flue. What is the concern?
o: None, because gas does not affect masonry
Acidic condensation from the flue gases may be deteriorating the chimney, and the debris can block the flue
The chimney is too short
The furnace needs a larger filter
en.e: Gas appliance exhaust contains water vapor that can condense in cool, unlined masonry flues and erode the mortar. A chimney professional should evaluate the chimney; a liner is often needed.

en.q: An oil-fired boiler has a heavy coating of soot around the burner and the flue pipe. What does this most likely indicate?
o: Incomplete combustion or draft problems that need service by a qualified technician
Normal operation for oil boilers
That the boiler is new
That the boiler is electric
en.e: Soot means fuel is not burning completely. That lowers efficiency and can block passages and create carbon monoxide. A technician should service the burner and check the draft.

en.q: A thermostat in an older house contains a small glass vial of silver liquid. Why might the inspector mention this?
o: The thermostat is solar powered
It is a mercury switch, which needs proper disposal if the thermostat is replaced
It is a gas leak indicator
It measures humidity
en.e: Older thermostats often use mercury switches. They work fine, but mercury is toxic, so the thermostat must be recycled properly when replaced.

en.q: What does a heat pump's reversing valve do?
o: It reduces water pressure in the system
It reverses the refrigerant flow so that the system can switch between heating and cooling
It turns the auxiliary heat on and off
It controls the humidifier
en.e: The reversing valve changes the direction of refrigerant flow, making the indoor coil the condenser in heating and the evaporator in cooling.

en.q: A bedroom has no heat supply register or other heat source. What should the inspector do?
o: Assume the room is heated by the rest of the house
Report that no heat source was observed in the habitable room
Recommend adding an unvented gas heater
Ignore it, because heat distribution is not inspected
en.e: Standards of practice include checking for the presence of an installed heat source in each room. Missing heat in a habitable room should be reported.

en.q: An inspector observes that a furnace vent connector has separated at a joint near the draft hood, and the screws are missing. What should be reported?
o: A cosmetic issue
A safety hazard, because combustion gases can leak into the house; recommend immediate correction by a qualified technician
Acceptable if the furnace runs
A defect only if the furnace is more than 20 years old
en.e: A disconnected or loose vent connector can spill carbon monoxide into living spaces. Vent connector joints must be secured as required (typically with screws or listed fasteners).

en.q: Per the IRC, what is the maximum riser height for stairs in a dwelling?
o: 7 inches
7-3/4 inches
8-1/4 inches
9 inches
en.e: Per the IRC (R311.7.5.1), the maximum riser height is 7-3/4 inches, measured vertically between the leading edges of adjacent treads.

en.q: Per the IRC, what is the minimum tread depth for stairs in a dwelling?
o: 9 inches
10 inches
11 inches
12 inches
en.e: Per the IRC (R311.7.5.2), the minimum tread depth is 10 inches, measured horizontally between the vertical planes of the foremost projections of adjacent treads.

en.q: Per the IRC, within one flight of stairs, the greatest riser height may exceed the smallest by no more than:
o: 1/8 inch
1/4 inch
3/8 inch
3/4 inch
en.e: Per the IRC (R311.7.5.1 and R311.7.5.2), the difference between the largest and smallest riser height, or tread depth, within a flight must not exceed 3/8 inch. Uneven steps are a major cause of falls.

en.q: On a basement stair, the bottom riser is 9 inches high while the others are about 7-1/2 inches. How should this be reported?
o: As acceptable, because only the top riser matters
As a trip hazard, because the riser exceeds the IRC maximum and the variation between risers is too great
As a cosmetic issue
As acceptable for basement stairs
en.e: The 9-inch riser exceeds the 7-3/4-inch maximum, and the 1-1/2-inch difference is far over the 3/8-inch limit. Users expect even steps, so this is a fall hazard.

en.q: Per the IRC, what is the minimum headroom over a stairway?
o: 6 feet 4 inches
6 feet 6 inches
6 feet 8 inches
7 feet
en.e: Per the IRC (R311.7.2), the minimum headroom is 6 feet 8 inches, measured vertically from the sloped plane along the tread nosings.

en.q: Per the IRC, what is the minimum clear width of a stairway above the handrail height?
o: 30 inches
36 inches
42 inches
48 inches
en.e: Per the IRC (R311.7.1), stairways must be at least 36 inches wide above the permitted handrail height. Handrails may project up to 4-1/2 inches on each side.

en.q: Per the IRC, handrails on stairs must be installed at what height, measured vertically from the sloped plane of the tread nosings?
o: 30 to 34 inches
34 to 38 inches
36 to 42 inches
38 to 44 inches
en.e: Per the IRC (R311.7.8.1), handrail height must be between 34 and 38 inches above the sloped plane of the nosings.

en.q: Per the IRC, a handrail must be provided on at least one side of a flight of stairs with how many risers?
o: 2 or more
3 or more
4 or more
6 or more
en.e: Per the IRC (R311.7.8), at least one handrail is required on each flight of stairs with four or more risers.

en.q: Per the IRC, a circular (Type I) handrail must have an outside diameter between:
o: 1-1/4 inches and 2 inches
1/2 inch and 1 inch
2-1/2 inches and 3 inches
3 inches and 4 inches
en.e: Per the IRC (R311.7.8.5), Type I handrails with a circular cross section must have an outside diameter of at least 1-1/4 inches and no more than 2 inches, so that the hand can grip them.

en.q: Per the IRC, what is the minimum clearance between a handrail and the wall?
o: 1/2 inch
1 inch
1-1/2 inches
3 inches
en.e: Per the IRC (R311.7.8.4), there must be at least 1-1/2 inches between the handrail and the wall or other surface so that fingers can wrap around it.

en.q: Per the IRC, what is the minimum height of a guard at an interior balcony or landing (not along the stairs)?
o: 30 inches
34 inches
36 inches
42 inches
en.e: Per the IRC (R312.1.2), guards must be at least 36 inches high, measured vertically from the walking surface. Guards along the open sides of stairs must be at least 34 inches high, measured from the nosings.

en.q: Per the IRC, the triangular opening formed by the riser, tread and bottom rail of a guard on the open side of a stair must not allow a sphere of what diameter to pass?
o: 4 inches
4-3/8 inches
6 inches
9 inches
en.e: Per the IRC (R312.1.3), the triangular openings at the open sides of stair treads must not pass a 6-inch sphere. Openings in the guard on the open sides of stairs must not pass a 4-3/8-inch sphere.

en.q: Per the IRC, guard openings on the open sides of stairs must not allow a sphere of what diameter to pass?
o: 4 inches
4-3/8 inches
5 inches
6 inches
en.e: Per the IRC (R312.1.3), guards on the open sides of stairs may not pass a 4-3/8-inch sphere; other guards may not pass a 4-inch sphere.

en.q: Per the IRC, what is the minimum net clear opening for an emergency escape and rescue window from a second-floor bedroom?
o: 4.4 square feet
5.0 square feet
5.7 square feet
9.0 square feet
en.e: Per the IRC (R310.2.1), emergency escape openings need at least 5.7 square feet of net clear opening. Openings at grade floor or below grade may be 5.0 square feet.

en.q: Per the IRC, an emergency escape window must have a net clear opening at least how high and how wide?
o: 20 inches high and 24 inches wide
24 inches high and 20 inches wide
30 inches high and 30 inches wide
36 inches high and 22 inches wide
en.e: Per the IRC (R310.2.1), the net clear opening height must be at least 24 inches and the width at least 20 inches. A window can meet both minimums and still fail the 5.7-square-foot area requirement.

en.q: Per the IRC, the bottom of the clear opening of an emergency escape window must be no more than how far above the floor?
o: 36 inches
44 inches
48 inches
60 inches
en.e: Per the IRC (R310.2.2), the sill height must not exceed 44 inches above the floor, measured to the bottom of the clear opening.

en.q: A basement bedroom's only window is a small hopper window with a sill 54 inches above the floor. What should be reported?
o: Nothing, because basement windows are exempt
The room lacks an adequate emergency escape opening; this is a safety hazard
The window needs a screen
The window should be painted shut for security
en.e: Every sleeping room, including those in basements, needs an emergency escape and rescue opening. A 54-inch sill exceeds the 44-inch limit, and a small hopper is unlikely to meet the size requirements.

en.q: Per the IRC, window fall protection is needed for an operable window when the sill is less than ___ above the floor and the window opening is more than ___ above the grade outside.
o: 18 inches; 48 inches
24 inches; 72 inches
36 inches; 60 inches
44 inches; 96 inches
en.e: Per the IRC (R312.2), where the bottom of the opening is less than 24 inches above the floor and more than 72 inches above grade, the opening must not pass a 4-inch sphere or must have approved fall-prevention or opening-control devices.

en.q: Per the IRC, which glazing is in a hazardous location and must be safety glazing (such as tempered glass)?
o: A kitchen window above the sink, 40 inches above the floor
A glass panel in a door
A small bathroom window 6 feet above the floor
A basement window 5 feet above the floor
en.e: Per the IRC (R308.4), glazing in doors is a hazardous location. Other examples include glazing within 24 inches of a door edge and near the floor, near tubs and showers, and large panes near walking surfaces.

en.q: Per the IRC, glazing in a wall enclosing a bathtub or shower is a hazardous location when its bottom edge is less than how far above the standing surface?
o: 36 inches
48 inches
60 inches
72 inches
en.e: Per the IRC (R308.4.5), glazing in walls and enclosures facing hot tubs, whirlpools, bathtubs and showers is hazardous where the bottom edge is less than 60 inches above the standing or walking surface.

en.q: Per the IRC, which of these is a hazardous location for glazing near a door?
o: Glazing within a 24-inch arc of either vertical edge of a closed door, with its bottom edge less than 60 inches above the floor
Glazing more than 10 feet from any door
Glazing more than 60 inches above the floor next to a door
Glazing in a decorative transom far above the door
en.e: Per the IRC (R308.4.2), glazing within a 24-inch arc of a door's vertical edge in the closed position, with its bottom less than 60 inches above the walking surface, requires safety glazing (with some exceptions).

en.q: How can an inspector usually confirm that a pane of glass is tempered?
o: By tapping it with a hammer
By finding the permanent safety-glazing label (etching) in a corner of the pane
By its color
By looking for small bubbles in the glass
en.e: Safety glazing is marked with a permanent label identifying it. Lack of a label where safety glazing is required should be reported, while noting that confirming the glass type is not always possible visually.

en.q: Per the IRC, where must smoke alarms be installed in a dwelling?
o: Only in the kitchen and living room
In each sleeping room, outside each separate sleeping area near the bedrooms, and on each additional story, including basements
Only at the top of the stairs
Only in the garage
en.e: Per the IRC (R314.3), smoke alarms are required in each sleeping room, outside each sleeping area in the immediate vicinity of the bedrooms, and on each additional story including basements and habitable attics (not crawl spaces or uninhabitable attics).

en.q: Per the IRC, smoke alarms must be installed at least how far horizontally from the door or opening of a bathroom that contains a tub or shower, unless this would prevent required placement?
o: 1 foot
3 feet
6 feet
10 feet
en.e: Per the IRC (R314.3), smoke alarms must be at least 3 feet horizontally from the door of a bathroom with a tub or shower, to reduce false alarms from steam.

en.q: Per the IRC, when must carbon monoxide alarms be installed in a dwelling?
o: In every dwelling, regardless of fuel
When the dwelling has fuel-fired appliances or an attached garage with an opening into the dwelling
Only in homes with a fireplace
Only in homes with a heat pump
en.e: Per the IRC (R315), CO alarms are required in dwellings with fuel-fired appliances or attached garages that open into the dwelling, outside each separate sleeping area in the immediate vicinity of the bedrooms, and in bedrooms with a fuel-fired appliance in the bedroom or its attached bathroom.

en.q: The smoke alarms in a house carry a manufacture date 14 years ago. What is the generally accepted recommendation?
o: They are fine until they stop beeping
Replace them, because smoke alarms should generally be replaced no later than 10 years after their manufacture date
Replace only their batteries
Paint them to make them work better
en.e: NFPA 72 and manufacturers call for replacing smoke alarms no more than 10 years after the date of manufacture, because sensors degrade over time.

en.q: Per the IRC, what is the minimum ceiling height for habitable rooms, hallways and bathrooms in general?
o: 6 feet 8 inches
7 feet
7 feet 6 inches
8 feet
en.e: Per the IRC (R305.1), habitable spaces, hallways, bathrooms, toilet rooms, laundry rooms and portions of basements containing these spaces need a ceiling height of at least 7 feet, with some exceptions such as for beams, sloped ceilings and bathroom fixtures.

en.q: Per the IRC, what is the minimum mechanical exhaust rate for a bathroom fan that runs intermittently, if the bathroom has no openable window meeting the IRC requirement?
o: 20 cfm
50 cfm
100 cfm
150 cfm
en.e: Per the IRC (R303.3 and Table M1505.4.4), bathrooms without an adequate openable window need exhaust of at least 50 cfm intermittent or 20 cfm continuous, discharged to the outdoors.

en.q: Per the IRC, what is the minimum exhaust rate for an intermittent kitchen range hood or kitchen exhaust fan?
o: 25 cfm
50 cfm
100 cfm
300 cfm
en.e: Per the IRC (Table M1505.4.4), kitchens need 100 cfm intermittent or 25 cfm continuous mechanical exhaust.

en.q: Per the IRC, what is the maximum developed length of a 4-inch clothes dryer exhaust duct, before deductions for fittings, when the manufacturer's instructions are not known?
o: 15 feet
25 feet
35 feet
50 feet
en.e: Per the IRC (M1502.4.5.1), the maximum length is 35 feet from the dryer to the outlet, reduced by 2.5 feet for each 45-degree bend and 5 feet for each 90-degree bend, unless the manufacturer allows more or a listed booster is used.

en.q: A dryer duct has three 90-degree elbows. Per the IRC's default rule, what is the maximum straight length that remains available?
o: 35 feet
27.5 feet
20 feet
15 feet
en.e: Each 90-degree bend deducts 5 feet: 35 minus (3 times 5) leaves 20 feet of duct. Long, twisting ducts trap lint and increase the fire risk.

en.q: A clothes dryer is connected to the wall with white vinyl flexible duct that runs inside a wall cavity. What is the concern?
o: Plastic flexible duct is not permitted for dryer exhaust and is a fire hazard; concealed transition ducts are also not allowed
None, because vinyl is fire-resistant
The duct is too short
The duct makes the dryer too quiet
en.e: Per the IRC (M1502), dryer exhaust ducts must be smooth metal, and the flexible transition duct must be listed, no more than 8 feet long and not concealed in construction. Plastic duct traps lint and burns.

en.q: Per the IRC, which feature is NOT permitted on a dryer exhaust termination?
o: A backdraft damper
A screen over the outlet
A termination outdoors
A hood that directs exhaust down and away
en.e: Per the IRC (M1502.3), dryer exhaust must terminate outdoors with a backdraft damper, and screens are prohibited because they catch lint and block the duct.

en.q: When the inspector opens the oven door and presses down lightly, the freestanding range tips forward. What is the most likely issue?
o: The oven is too heavy
The anti-tip bracket is missing or not engaged
The floor is sloped toward the wall
The range has no gas shut-off
en.e: Ranges are required to be installed with anti-tip devices, because a child standing on an open oven door can tip the range and be burned or crushed. A missing bracket is a safety item.

en.q: A double-pane window has a permanent fogged haze between the panes that cannot be wiped off. What does this indicate?
o: Normal condensation on the inside surface
A failed seal in the insulated glass unit
A cracked window frame
Too much humidity outdoors
en.e: Moisture between the panes means the seal has failed, reducing the window's insulating value and clarity. InterNACHI's standards call for reporting windows that are obviously fogged.
