en.q: Brown stains on a ceiling below a bathroom are dry to the touch, and the moisture meter shows normal readings at the time of inspection. What is the most appropriate report entry?
o: State that the leak has been repaired
Leave it out of the report because it is dry
Report the stains, note that they were dry at the time of inspection, and recommend asking the seller about their history or further evaluation
State that the stain is from mold
en.e: An inspector cannot tell from a dry stain whether the leak is fixed or intermittent. Reporting what was observed and what could not be determined protects the client.

en.q: Under typical standards of practice, is the home inspector required to identify mold?
o: Yes, and must take air samples
No; mold and other environmental hazards are excluded, though visible signs of moisture damage or suspected growth may be reported
Yes, but only in basements
Only if the inspector sees it in the attic
en.e: Standards of practice exclude determining the presence of mold or other environmental hazards. Inspectors can still describe moisture problems and suspected growth and recommend evaluation by a qualified professional.

en.q: What is the generally recommended indoor relative humidity range for homes to limit both condensation and dryness?
o: 5 to 15 percent
About 30 to 50 percent
60 to 80 percent
90 to 100 percent
en.e: Agencies such as the EPA recommend keeping indoor relative humidity roughly between 30 and 50 percent (and below 60 percent) to limit mold, dust mites and condensation.

en.q: What does R-value measure in insulation?
o: The weight of the insulation
Resistance to heat flow; a higher R-value insulates better
The amount of radon the material blocks
The material's moisture content
en.e: R-value measures thermal resistance. It depends on material type and thickness, and compressing or wetting insulation reduces its effective R-value.

en.q: In a crawl space under a heated floor, kraft-faced fiberglass batts are installed with the paper facing down toward the crawl space soil. What is the concern?
o: None, because facing direction never matters
The vapor retarder is on the cold side instead of the warm-in-winter side, which can trap moisture in the insulation
The batts will be too warm
The facing will attract termites
en.e: Vapor retarders belong on the warm-in-winter side of the insulation in most climates; for a floor over a crawl space that is the subfloor side. Facing the wrong way can trap moisture.

en.q: Recessed light fixtures in a ceiling below the attic are buried in loose-fill insulation, and the fixtures are not IC-rated. What is the concern?
o: Non-IC fixtures can overheat and create a fire hazard when covered by insulation
They will make the room too dark
They will cause the insulation to blow away
None, because insulation is fire-proof
en.e: Only IC-rated (insulation contact) fixtures may be covered by insulation. Non-IC fixtures need clearance from insulation (commonly 3 inches) or replacement with IC-rated units.

en.q: Loose, pebble-like, gray-brown insulation with a shiny look is found between attic joists. What is the most appropriate report statement?
o: That it is rock wool and harmless
That it appears to be vermiculite, which may contain asbestos; it should not be disturbed, and testing by a qualified professional is recommended
That it must be removed by the client immediately
That it is cellulose insulation
en.e: Much of the vermiculite sold in North America (such as Zonolite) came from a mine contaminated with asbestos. The EPA advises leaving it undisturbed and using trained professionals if it must be removed.

en.q: Per the IRC, what minimum hearth extension is required in front of a masonry fireplace with a fireplace opening smaller than 6 square feet?
o: 8 inches in front and 6 inches on each side
16 inches in front and 8 inches on each side
20 inches in front and 12 inches on each side
24 inches in front and 16 inches on each side
en.e: Per the IRC (R1001.10), hearth extensions must extend at least 16 inches in front of and 8 inches beyond each side of the opening. If the opening is 6 square feet or larger, it is 20 inches in front and 12 inches on each side.

en.q: Per the IRC, a masonry fireplace opening is 7 square feet. What minimum hearth extension is required?
o: 16 inches in front and 8 inches on each side
20 inches in front and 12 inches on each side
24 inches in front and 16 inches on each side
36 inches in front and 18 inches on each side
en.e: Per the IRC (R1001.10), when the fireplace opening is 6 square feet or larger, the hearth extension must be at least 20 inches in front and 12 inches on each side.

en.q: Per the IRC, a masonry chimney must extend at least how far above the highest point where it passes through the roof, and how much higher than any part of the building within 10 feet?
o: 1 foot above the roof; 1 foot higher than the building within 10 feet
2 feet above the roof; 3 feet higher than the building within 10 feet
3 feet above the roof; 2 feet higher than the building within 10 feet
5 feet above the roof; 5 feet higher than the building within 10 feet
en.e: Per the IRC (R1003.9), chimneys must extend at least 3 feet above the highest point where they pass through the roof and at least 2 feet higher than any part of the building within 10 feet horizontally.

en.q: Per the IRC, what is the minimum depth of the firebox of a masonry fireplace (other than a Rumford fireplace)?
o: 12 inches
16 inches
20 inches
30 inches
en.e: Per the IRC (R1001.6), the firebox must be at least 20 inches deep. Rumford fireplaces may be 12 inches deep if they meet specific proportions.

en.q: Per the IRC, wood mantels and other combustible trim must be kept at least how far from a masonry fireplace opening?
o: 2 inches
6 inches
12 inches
18 inches
en.e: Per the IRC (R1001.11), combustible materials must not be within 6 inches of the fireplace opening. Combustibles within 12 inches of the opening may not project more than 1/8 inch for each 1 inch of distance from the opening.

en.q: Per the IRC, what airspace clearance is required between combustible framing and the outside of a masonry chimney located inside the exterior walls?
o: No clearance
2 inches
6 inches
12 inches
en.e: Per the IRC (R1003.18), masonry chimneys need 2 inches of clearance to combustibles when inside the exterior walls of the building, and 1 inch when entirely outside the exterior walls.

en.q: NFPA 211 recommends which level of chimney inspection when a property is sold or transferred?
o: Level I
Level II
Level III
No inspection is recommended
en.e: NFPA 211 calls for a Level II inspection upon sale or transfer of a property, after an operating malfunction or external event, or when changes are made to the system. A Level II includes a video scan of the flue.

en.q: The inspector sees black staining on the face of the brick above a fireplace opening. What does this most likely indicate?
o: Smoke spilling into the room, suggesting a draft problem
The fireplace is new
Normal wear from cleaning the brick
A gas leak
en.e: Soot staining above the opening usually means smoke is escaping into the room, from causes such as an undersized flue, a short chimney, a closed or damaged damper, or low house pressure. A chimney professional should evaluate it.

en.q: Under typical home inspection standards of practice, a home inspection is best described as:
o: A technically exhaustive engineering evaluation of every system
A guarantee that the house has no hidden defects
A non-invasive visual examination of readily accessible systems and components, reported as of the time of inspection
A code compliance inspection for the local building department
en.e: Standards such as ASHI's and InterNACHI's define a home inspection as a non-invasive, visual examination of readily accessible components. It is not technically exhaustive and does not guarantee against concealed defects.

en.q: Under ASHI's definitions, "readily accessible" means available for visual inspection:
o: Without moving personal property, dismantling, destructive measures or actions likely to involve risk to persons or property
After moving any furniture the client requests
Only with the help of a ladder longer than 20 feet
Only after removing finished wall surfaces
en.e: Inspectors are not required to move belongings, dismantle components or take risky or destructive actions. Areas that are blocked or unsafe are reported as not inspected.

en.q: Under ASHI's standard of practice, a "representative number" of multiple similar interior components, such as windows and receptacles, means:
o: Every one of them
Half of them
One component per room
Only those the seller points out
en.e: ASHI defines a representative number as one component per room for multiple similar interior components and one on each side of the building for multiple similar exterior components.

en.q: Under typical standards of practice, when the inspector does not inspect a system or component that is normally included, what must the report state?
o: Nothing, because the client will assume it was skipped
That it was not inspected and the reason it was not inspected
That it is in good condition
That the seller is responsible for it
en.e: Standards of practice require reporting systems and components that were not inspected and why, such as being inaccessible, shut down or unsafe to reach.

en.q: The water is shut off at the main valve in a vacant, bank-owned house. What is the most appropriate action?
o: Turn the main valve on and inspect the plumbing
Report that the plumbing system is in good condition
Leave the valve closed, report that the plumbing could not be fully tested and why, and recommend inspection once the water is restored
Refund the inspection fee
en.e: Standards of practice do not require operating shut-off valves or systems that are shut down. Turning on water in a winterized or neglected house can cause flooding, so the limitation is reported instead.

en.q: Under typical standards of practice, which is the inspector NOT required to determine?
o: Whether the water heater has a TPR valve
Whether the house complies with current building codes
Whether visible guards have wide openings
Whether the furnace responds to normal controls
en.e: Home inspections are not code inspections. Inspectors may use codes as a reference for safety, but determining code compliance is excluded from standards of practice.

en.q: A buyer asks the inspector how much it will cost to replace the roof. Under typical standards of practice, what is the most appropriate response?
o: Give an exact price
Explain that cost estimates are outside the inspection and suggest getting quotes from qualified roofers
Refuse to discuss the roof at all
Tell the buyer to ask the seller for a credit of a specific amount
en.e: Standards of practice exclude determining the cost of repairs. Inspectors identify and report conditions; contractors provide estimates.

en.q: At the end of the inspection, the buyer asks, "Should I buy this house?" What is the most appropriate response?
o: "Yes, it's a great house"
"No, walk away"
Explain that advising on whether to buy is outside the inspector's role, and help the client understand the findings so they can decide
Recommend a lower purchase price
en.e: Standards of practice exclude advising on the advisability of purchase and market value. The inspector's job is to explain the findings clearly.

en.q: Under both the ASHI and InterNACHI codes of ethics, an inspector must not perform or offer to perform repairs on a home they inspected, for compensation, for how long after the inspection?
o: 30 days
90 days
12 months (one year)
Five years
en.e: Both codes of ethics prohibit performing or offering repairs on systems or components covered by the inspection for 12 months (one year) after the inspection, to avoid a conflict of interest.

en.q: A real estate agent offers an inspector $50 for every client the agent refers. What is the most appropriate response under typical codes of ethics?
o: Accept, because referral fees are standard
Decline, because accepting compensation from parties with an interest in the sale is a conflict of interest
Accept, but only for high-priced homes
Accept the money and not tell the client
en.e: Codes of ethics prohibit accepting commissions, fees or other compensation from real estate agents or other parties with an interest in the transaction, because it can bias the report.

en.q: An inspector's brother-in-law is the listing agent for a house a client wants inspected. What should the inspector do?
o: Inspect without mentioning it
Disclose the relationship to the client before accepting the inspection, so the client can decide
Give the brother-in-law a copy of the report first
Refuse to inspect any house in the city
en.e: Codes of ethics require inspectors to disclose any conflict of interest, such as a family or financial relationship with a party to the transaction, before the inspection.

en.q: The seller asks the inspector for a copy of the buyer's inspection report. What should the inspector do?
o: Send it immediately, because the seller owns the house
Provide it only with the client's permission, unless the law requires otherwise
Send the seller a summary but not the full report
Post the report online
en.e: The report belongs to the client. Codes of ethics prohibit disclosing inspection results without the client's approval, except where required by law or for an immediate safety hazard.

en.q: Under ASHI's code of ethics, when may an inspector disclose an observed immediate safety hazard to someone other than the client?
o: To occupants who are exposed to the hazard, when feasible
Never, under any circumstances
Only after the closing
Only to the real estate agent
en.e: ASHI's code allows inspectors, at their discretion, to disclose observed immediate safety hazards to occupants exposed to them, when feasible.

en.q: After the inspection, the listing agent asks the inspector to delete a comment about a missing GFCI because it might "upset the buyer." What should the inspector do?
o: Delete it to keep the agent happy
Change the wording to say it is optional
Refuse, because the report is for the client and must reflect the inspector's honest findings
Remove it only from the summary page
en.e: The inspector's duty is to the client. Altering findings at the request of another party would be unethical. Corrections are made only for genuine factual errors.

en.q: Which report comment is the best example of clear, useful report writing?
o: "Electrical issues noted."
"Monitor the roof."
"The upstairs hall bathroom receptacle did not trip when tested and is not GFCI-protected. This is a shock hazard. Recommend correction by a licensed electrician."
"Some things might need work; consult a pro."
en.e: A good comment states what was found, where it is, why it matters and what to do and by whom. Vague phrases like "issues noted" or "monitor" leave the client without useful guidance.

en.q: What is the main problem with ending a report comment with "monitor" for a structural crack?
o: It is too specific
It shifts responsibility to the client without guidance, and the client may not know what to watch or when to act
It is required by all standards
It makes the report too long
en.e: "Monitor" alone gives no criteria. If the condition matters, the better approach is to describe it and recommend evaluation by a qualified professional.

en.q: The inspector sees stains and soft drywall under a window but is not sure of the cause. What is the best reporting approach?
o: Guess the cause and state it as fact
Leave it out because the cause is unknown
Describe what was observed and where, explain the possible significance, and recommend further evaluation
Tell the client it is probably nothing
en.e: Inspectors are not required to determine causes, but they must report significant findings. Describing the observation and recommending evaluation is accurate and defensible.

en.q: Under ASHI's definitions, "further evaluation" means:
o: Asking the inspector to return the next day
Examination and analysis by a qualified professional, tradesman or service technician beyond what the home inspection provides
The client looking at the item again
A second inspection by the same inspector at no cost
en.e: Recommending further evaluation tells the client a specialist is needed to diagnose the condition, its cause and the repair.

en.q: When should the pre-inspection agreement (contract) ideally be signed?
o: After the report is delivered
At the closing
Before the inspection begins
Only if there is a dispute
en.e: A signed pre-inspection agreement defines the scope, limitations, fee and terms before work starts, which protects both the client and the inspector.

en.q: What does a pre-inspection agreement typically include?
o: A guarantee that the house has no defects
The scope of the inspection, exclusions and limitations, the fee, and terms such as dispute resolution
The repair price for each defect
The appraised value of the home
en.e: The agreement sets expectations by defining what is and is not included, referencing the standard of practice and stating business terms.

en.q: In a negligence claim against a home inspector, which four elements generally must the client prove?
o: Fraud, intent, malice and damages
Duty, breach of duty, causation and damages
Price, location, timing and age of the house
Contract, signature, payment and receipt
en.e: Negligence requires a duty owed, a breach of the standard of care, a causal link between the breach and the harm, and actual damages.

en.q: What type of insurance mainly covers claims that the inspector missed or misreported a defect?
o: General liability insurance
Errors and omissions (professional liability) insurance
Workers' compensation insurance
Auto insurance
en.e: E&O insurance covers claims of professional negligence, such as missed defects. General liability covers bodily injury and property damage, such as breaking a window during the inspection.

en.q: While opening an attic hatch, the inspector accidentally cracks a ceiling light fixture. Which insurance would typically cover this?
o: General liability insurance
Errors and omissions insurance
Health insurance
Title insurance
en.e: General liability insurance covers physical damage to property and bodily injury that happen during the inspector's work. E&O covers errors in professional judgment and reporting.

en.q: Why do inspectors typically include a limitation of liability clause in their agreement?
o: To avoid any duty to the client
To limit the inspector's financial exposure, often to the inspection fee, where state law allows such clauses
To guarantee the client full replacement cost for any missed defect
To prevent the client from reading the report
en.e: Limitation of liability clauses try to cap damages. Their enforceability varies by state, and some states restrict or prohibit them for home inspectors.

en.q: What should an inspector record about conditions on the day of inspection?
o: Only the client's name
Weather and other conditions that limited the inspection, such as rain, snow cover, outdoor temperature or utilities that were off
The seller's reasons for selling
The real estate commission
en.e: Conditions affect what can be seen and tested. Recording them explains limitations, such as not testing air conditioning in cold weather or not seeing a snow-covered roof.

en.q: The house is full of stored boxes that block access to the basement walls and the electrical panel. What should the inspector do?
o: Move all the boxes and inspect behind them
Inspect what is accessible, and report the areas that were blocked and that defects could be hidden there
Report the house as having no basement defects
Cancel the inspection without explanation
en.e: Standards of practice do not require moving personal property. The report should clearly state the limitations so that the client can arrange access if needed.

en.q: Per OSHA guidance, an extension ladder should be set up so that its base is about how far from the wall for every 4 feet of ladder height to the support point?
o: 6 inches
1 foot
2 feet
4 feet
en.e: The 4-to-1 rule puts the base 1 foot out for every 4 feet of working height. Ladders used to reach a roof should also extend at least 3 feet above the roof edge.

en.q: When a ladder is used to access a roof, how far should it extend above the roof edge?
o: 1 foot
3 feet
5 feet
It should stop just below the gutter
en.e: Extending the ladder at least 3 feet above the landing surface gives a handhold for getting on and off the roof safely, per OSHA guidance.

en.q: An aggressive dog is loose in the crawl space access area. What should the inspector do?
o: Enter anyway
Not enter the area, report that it was not inspected because of the unsafe condition, and offer to return if the situation changes
Use the dog as an excuse to skip the whole inspection
Ask the client to remove the dog
en.e: Inspectors are not required to enter areas that are unsafe. The limitation is reported, and a return visit can be arranged.

en.q: Which of these is a sound reason to include photographs in an inspection report?
o: To help the client understand the location and nature of findings
To replace written descriptions entirely
To show the seller's belongings
To make the report longer
en.e: Photos support but do not replace written descriptions. They help clients and contractors find and understand the conditions.

en.q: A client asks the inspector to test the home for radon as part of the inspection. What is the appropriate approach?
o: Radon is always included in a home inspection
Radon testing is an ancillary service outside the standard of practice; the inspector may offer it if properly trained, and certified or licensed where required
Tell the client that radon is not a real concern
Estimate the radon level by looking at the basement
en.e: Environmental testing such as radon is excluded from standards of practice but may be offered as an added service with proper training and any required credentials, using approved test protocols.

en.q: Under typical standards of practice, the inspector is NOT required to report on:
o: Safety hazards observed
Components not functioning properly
The remaining service life of systems and components
Systems that were not inspected and why
en.e: Inspectors report deficiencies and safety issues but are not required to predict remaining life. They may note when a system appears near the end of its typical service life.

en.q: During the walkthrough, the inspector tells the client the roof "looks fine," but the written report later describes significant roof damage. What is the main risk?
o: None, because only the verbal comments count
Conflicting statements can confuse the client and create liability; verbal and written findings should agree
The client will read the report faster
The report will be shorter
en.e: Inconsistent communication undermines trust and can lead to claims. Inspectors should be careful that on-site comments match the written report.

en.q: What is a key reason inspectors should avoid citing specific code sections as requirements in their reports?
o: Codes do not exist for homes
Home inspections are not code inspections; the code that applied when the house was built may differ, and the jurisdiction decides compliance
Clients prefer longer explanations
Codes are secret
en.e: Inspectors can explain why a condition is unsafe or improper, sometimes referencing generally accepted practice, but they do not determine code compliance.

en.q: A newly built home is being inspected before closing. The builder says the city already inspected it, so the inspector should skip the attic. What should the inspector do?
o: Skip the attic as requested
Inspect the attic as agreed with the client, because municipal inspections do not replace the client's home inspection
Ask the builder to inspect the attic instead
Report the attic as acceptable without looking
en.e: The inspector works for the client and follows the agreed scope. Code inspections check different things, and new homes can have significant defects.

en.q: Which statement about InterNACHI's definition of a "material defect" is most accurate?
o: Any cosmetic flaw is a material defect
A specific issue that may significantly affect the value of the property or that poses an unreasonable risk to people
Only defects that cost more than $10,000
Any item the seller has disclosed
en.e: InterNACHI defines a material defect as a specific issue with a system or component that may have a significant, adverse impact on the property's value, or that poses an unreasonable risk to people. Age or end of service life alone is not necessarily a material defect.

en.q: The client asks the inspector to certify that the house will have no problems for five years. What is the correct response?
o: Agree, for an extra fee
Explain that a home inspection is not a warranty or guarantee and reports conditions only at the time of inspection
Agree, but only for the roof
Refuse to perform the inspection
en.e: Standards of practice state the inspection is not a warranty or guarantee. Some inspectors partner with third-party warranty providers, but the inspection itself does not guarantee future performance.

en.q: A probing awl is pushed into a finished, painted wood baseboard that looks sound, just to check. Under ASHI's standard, why is this inappropriate?
o: Probing is never allowed
Probing is not required where it would damage a finished surface or where no deterioration is visible or presumed
Probing must be done only with a moisture meter
Probing is required on all surfaces
en.e: ASHI calls for probing structural components where deterioration is suspected, but not where probing would damage finished surfaces or where no deterioration is visible or presumed.

en.q: An inspector discovers wiring that is energized and exposed in a reachable location in an occupied home. What is the best course of action?
o: Inform the client and, where feasible, the occupants of the immediate hazard, and report it clearly as a safety issue
Fix the wiring personally
Keep it secret until the report is delivered
Turn off the main power to the house and leave
en.e: Immediate hazards should be communicated promptly. Ethics codes allow disclosure to exposed occupants. The inspector should not perform repairs.

en.q: An inspector's fee is set so that it is higher if more defects are found. Why is this a problem?
o: It makes the report shorter
It creates a conflict of interest, because the inspector benefits financially from the findings
It is required by most standards
It lowers the inspector's insurance costs
en.e: Compensation that depends on the inspection's findings, or on whether the sale closes, gives the inspector a motive to slant the report. Fees should be independent of the findings.

en.q: Under InterNACHI's standards, which of these is the inspector NOT required to do?
o: Report the method used to inspect the attic
Describe the type of heating system
Report as in need of correction any heating system that did not operate
Move insulation to inspect framing beneath it
en.e: Inspectors are not required to move insulation, personal items or debris that obstruct access. The resulting limitation is reported.

en.q: On the National Home Inspector Examination, how many of the 200 questions are unscored pretest items?
o: None
en.e: EBPHI states that 25 of the 200 questions are pretest items being evaluated for future use. They are not scored and are not identified, so 175 questions count.

en.q: What score is needed to pass the National Home Inspector Examination?
o: 70 percent of all questions
A scaled score of 500 on a scale of 200 to 800
A raw score of 150
80 percent of the scored questions
en.e: EBPHI reports NHIE results as a scaled score from 200 to 800, with 500 as the passing point. Scaling keeps results comparable across different forms of the exam.

en.q: On the current NHIE content outline, which domain carries the most weight?
o: Property and Building Inspection/Site Review
Analysis of Findings and Reporting
Professional Responsibilities
Business Marketing
en.e: On the current EBPHI outline, Domain 1, Property and Building Inspection/Site Review, is about 70% of the scored questions. Analysis of Findings and Reporting is about 20%, and Professional Responsibilities about 10%.

en.q: A client calls a week after the inspection and asks a question about the report. What is the best practice?
o: Ignore the call, because the job is finished
Answer the client's questions and clarify the report, keeping the answer consistent with the written findings
Charge a full new inspection fee to answer
Tell the client to ask the seller
en.e: Good client service includes explaining the report after delivery. Answers should be consistent with the written report; any changes should be documented properly.

en.q: Which of these best describes the inspector's main duty under typical standards of practice?
o: To negotiate repairs with the seller
To observe, describe and report on the condition of readily accessible systems and components for the client
To approve the mortgage loan
To appraise the home's value
en.e: The inspector's role is to inspect and report objectively for the client. Negotiation, lending and appraisal are other professionals' roles.

en.q: Two days before the inspection, the inspector is asked by a homeowner to pre-inspect the house and then also inspect it for the buyer, for two fees, without telling either party. Why is this improper?
o: It is not improper
Codes of ethics prohibit accepting compensation from more than one party for the same service without the informed consent of all parties
The inspector must charge both parties the same fee
The buyer's inspection must happen first
en.e: ASHI's code says inspectors must not accept compensation from more than one party for the same service without the consent of all parties. Undisclosed dual roles create conflicts of interest.

en.q: Which wording best describes a safety concern without overstating it?
o: "This will definitely cause a fire."
"Overheated wiring was observed at the breaker. This is a potential fire hazard; recommend evaluation and repair by a licensed electrician."
"Wiring seems okay, probably."
"Electrical system condemned."
en.e: Good reporting states the observation, explains the potential consequence and recommends the right professional, without exaggerated predictions or vague minimization.

en.q: An inspector cannot access the attic because the only hatch is sealed shut with paint and caulk. What is the most appropriate action?
o: Cut the hatch open with a utility knife
Report that the attic was not inspected because the access was sealed, and recommend inspection once access is available
Assume the attic is in good condition
Inspect the attic from the roof vents
en.e: Breaking seals or damaging finishes is destructive and outside the standard. Reporting the limitation and recommending access is the correct approach.

en.q: Why is it important for a report to separate safety hazards and significant defects from minor maintenance items?
o: So that the report can skip minor items
So that the client can quickly see the conditions that most affect safety and the decision to buy
Because standards require only safety items
So that the seller pays for maintenance items
en.e: Organizing findings by significance helps the client focus on what matters most, while the full report still lists the minor items.
